questions.stem: With regard to the parenteral administration of branched chain amino acids (BCAA):
options: A. BCAA administration to catabolic surgical patients enhances the quality and number of polyribosomes in skeletal muscle.
B. BCAA administration improves patient outcome after major hepatic surgery.
C. BCAA are mainly metabolised in the liver.
D. There is no role for parenteral BCAA therapy in patients with hepatic encephalopathy.
E. When used clinically, BCAA should be administered at a dose of 0.1 to 0.3 g/kg/d.
questions.explanation: The BCAA - leucine, isoleucine, and valine - are essential amino acids required for protein synthetic functions. BCAA are primarily metabolised by skeletal muscle, rather than the liver. When given in a balanced amino acid formulation at a dose of 0.5 to 1.2 g/kg/d BCAA can improve nitrogen retention and increase protein synthetic functions relative to standard amino acids formulations e.g. the number and quality of polyribosomes in skeletal muscle. As illustrated, BCAA can be consumed in muscle to generate glutamine. Nevertheless, their exact role in promoting improved patient outcomes in surgical patients remains to be defined. But it is clear that, in patients who are protein-intolerant because of chronic or latent hepatic encephalopathy, BCAA-enriched parenteral nutrition permit greater protein intake without inducing encephalopathy than do standard protein formulas.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: With regard to arginine:
options: A. When administered in pharmacological doses arginine may act as a neuotransmitter.
B. Alanine is the main precursor of arginine.
C. Critically ill patients require 30 g/day of arginine.
D. Arginine is a unique substrate for the production of nitric oxide.
E. Arginine is the preferred nutrient for immunocytes.
questions.explanation: Arginine is now considered to be a conditionally essential amino acid. Arginine is synthesised endogenously in the kidney from gut-derived citrulline (the small intestine converts dietary amino acids, including glutamine, to citrulline). Arginine participates in a variety of metabolic functions, including urea synthesis, lymphocyte proliferation, and wound healing. In addition, arginine is a unique substrate for the production of the biologic effector molecule, nitric oxide. This important pathway has been shown to be present in many tissues and cells including endothelium and inflammatory cells. The role of arginine in critically ill patients remain to be defined but doses of up to 30 g/day have been used in evaluative studies. Combinations of nutrients with immune function activity - arginine, fish oil, and nucleic acids - are being evaluated as enteral nutrients in critically ill patients: although they are sometimes referred to as 'immunonutrients', their clinical efficacy has yet to be confirmed by independent clinical trials.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: With regard to glutamine:
options: A. Glutamine is the only amino acid that contains three nitrogen molecules.
B. Glutamine constitutes about 25% of the amino acid content of standard solutions of parenteral nutrients.
C. Critically ill patients require 20 g/day of glutamine.
D. Glutamine is the principal fuel used by rapidly proliferating cells.
E. The kidney consumes glutamine during periods of metabolic alkalosis.
questions.explanation: We discussed the metabolism of glutamine in Topic 1. It is the main fuel consumed by rapidly dividin cells such as the gut mucosa, immunocytes, and some tumours. Glutamine is not included in standard solutions of parenteral nutrients because it is unstable in solution and breaks down to form toxic amounts of pyroglutamate and ammonia. It remains to be determined whether administering glutamine to catabolic patients results in an improved outcome. As mentioned in Topic 1, the kidney consumes glutamine during periods of metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: With regard to albumin:
options: A. Serum concentrations < 30 g/L strongly correlate with a poor clinical outcome.
B. It is a useful marker of nutritional status because it has a relatively short half-life.
C. Synthesis is markedly inhibited during the early stages of undernutrition.
D. It has a low exchange rate between the intra- and extra-vascular compartments.
E. Serum concentrations are increased during sepsis.
questions.explanation: Hepatic secretory proteins such as albumin, transferrin, retinol binding protein, and prealbumin are markers of visceral protein stores and are used as indicators of nutritional status. Numerous studies have demonstrated that a low serum albumin concentration ( < 30 g/L) strongly correlates with a high incidence of mortality and morbidity. However, albumin has a half-life of about 28 days and acute changes in serum albumin concentration cannot be ascribed to poor nutrition. For example, serum albumin concentrations are usually not affected by nutritional intake during starvation until starvation has reached an advanced stage and there is a marked reduction in body weight accompanied by overt muscle wasting. On the other hand, the low serum albumin concentrations that are observed in stressed patients persist until the parts start to recover and there is an absence of inflammatory foci. The exchange rate between intravascular and extravascular albumin is large and even small variations in the percentage of exchange can cause significant changes in serum albumin concentration. Levels of regulatory hormones, acute-phase reactants, and the measurement of the circulating levels of a number of cytokines have also been proposed as 'nutritional markers'. For example, C-reactive protein has the attraction of being present in very low concentrations in the serum of normal subjects, but rising exponentially within four hours of the onset of infection. However such measurements reflect metabolic stress rather than nutritional status. HAEMATOLOGY

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Heparin and warfarin have significant similarities in mechanism of action but the action of aspirin is different
statements.explanation: Heparin (via antithrombin III potentiation) and warfarin (via inhibition of vitamin K-dependent clotting factor activation) both act on the clotting cascade, while aspirin instead inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase and platelet aggregation, a genuinely different mechanism.

statements.text: platelets have no influence on the clotting cascade.
statements.explanation: Platelets do influence the clotting cascade: platelet phospholipids are essential cofactors for several steps of the cascade occurring on the platelet surface, so the claim that platelets have no influence on clotting is false.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation by inhibiting cyclo- oxygenase activity
statements.explanation: Aspirin inhibits cyclo-oxygenase activity in platelets, reducing production of the endoperoxides and thromboxane A2 needed to promote vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, thereby decreasing platelet aggregability.

statements.text: cyclo-oxygenase converts arachidonic acid to endoperoxides PGG2 and PGH2
statements.explanation: Cyclo-oxygenase converts arachidonic acid into endoperoxides PGG2 and PGH2, some of which is further converted by thromboxane synthetase into thromboxane A2 in platelets, providing the mechanistic basis for aspirin's antiplatelet effect.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Which of the following is an enzyme?
questions.explanation: The nonapeptide bradykinin is one of the vasodilator peptides formed in the plasma. The octapeptide angiotensin II is the most potent vasoconstrictor known and acts directly on the adrenal cortex, on peripheral noradrenergic neurons, and on water metabolism as well. The nonapeptide vasopressin (ADH) is one of the two posterior pituitary gland hormones. Its main physiologic effect is the retention of water by the kidney. Gastrin is a polypeptide hormone produced by the G cells of the gastric antral mucosa. Its principal action is stimulation of gastric acid and pepsin secretion. The above mentioned four physiologically active peptides (or polypeptides) have no enzymatic activity (A, B, C and D false). Renin is a proteolytic enzyme secreted by the kidney into the bloodstream, with a molecular weight of 40 000 in humans. It splits the end off one of the plasma proteins called renin substrate, to release a decapeptide, angiotensin I (E true).

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow has all the following characteristics except
options: A. high oxygen extraction fraction of about 70% at rest
B. nearly 100% oxygen extraction during exercise
C. a large increase in flow, up to five or six times, during maximal exercise
D. limitation of increased flow in exercise in the presence of proximal stenoses
E. flow peaking during systole when the driving pressure is greatest
questions.explanation: The heart is extremely aerobic, burning fatty acids, ketones and some glucose continuously. The extraction fraction is large at rest, and can therefore be increased only moderately, so that increased oxygen delivery during exercise depends on increased flow. For the left ventricle, pressure within the myocardium limits flow during systole. Maximal flow occurs during diastole, so E, being incorrect, is the required answer.

questions.stem: In a failing left ventricle all of the following parameters are reduced except
options: C. rate of rise of pressure (dP/dt) at the commencement of systole
D. stroke-volume at a given filling pressure
E. systolic shortening of myocardial fibre length
questions.explanation: The biochemical changes in a failing ventricle lead to a shift of the Starling curve (stroke volume versus filling pressure) to the right. Changes in expression of myosin isoforms results in slower contraction with reduced dP/dt, which is an important index of ventricular function derived during catheter studies. Stroke volume is reduced at each value of filling pressure, so that systolic fibre length shortening is reduced, ejection fraction falls, and end systolic volume increases. Thus B, being incorrect, is the required answer.

questions.topic_label: Cardiovascular Physiology — Heart as a Pump
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Isometric contraction of the left ventricle
options: A. occurs during the first third of systole
B. involves the most rapid change in pressure per unit time in the cardiac cycle
C. occurs after closure of the aortic valve
D. is terminated at the T wave of the ECG
E. is responsible for ejection of a majority of the stroke volume
questions.explanation: During the cardiac cycle, the time sequence is: diastolic filling (with atrial systole in late diastole increasing filling); the QRS complex; ventricular contraction commencing at the peak of the R wave; A-V valve closure; isometric ventricular contraction (isometric means equal size: the volume does not change) with rapidly rising ventricular pressure; opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves as the ventricular pressure exceeds arterial diastolic pressure; rapid ejection in the first third of systole; slow ejection; the T wave; ventricular relaxation with falling ventricular pressure; aortic and pulmonary valve closure and the dicrotic notch in the arterial pressure waveform; isometric relaxation; opening of the A-V valves; rapid phase of diastolic filling. Isometric contraction occurs at the commencement of systole, does not involve any ejection of blood, and is the steepest part of the pressure-time graph. Answer B is the only one correct.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Patients with severe aortic stenosis causing left ventricular failure have poor outcomes from valvular surgery
statements.explanation: Aortic valve surgery typically improves cardiac status dramatically by relieving the pressure gradient across the valve and reducing cardiac workload, so outcomes are not generally poor; this statement is false.

statements.text: impaired left ventricular function may persist after correction of the stenosis.
statements.explanation: Long-term changes from pressure-overload failure, including pathological hypertrophy, fibrosis, vascular insufficiency and altered myosin isoform expression, may persist after the stenosis is corrected, but this is a true fact on its own rather than an explanation for poor surgical outcomes.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: In a patient with mixed aortic stenosis and insufficiency due to rheumatic heart disease, deteriorating cardiac function could be exacerbated by all except
options: A. increased pressure gradient across the aortic valve
B. increased reflux through the aortic valve
questions.explanation: Cardiac workload is increased by both volume and pressure overload in valve disease. Systemic hypertension will add to the pressure workload and is a well-known, correctable factor in cardiac failure. The diastolic pressure has other implications, however. Because of the intramural pressure increase during systole, most of the left ventricular coronary blood flow occurs during diastole: therefore, diastolic pressure and time are important. The reduced aortic diastolic pressure seen with aortic incompetence will seriously compromise coronary flow. Thus, C is the only factor that improves rather than worsens the patient's cardiac function, and is therefore the required answer.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Essential differences between cardiac failure with diastolic dysfunction and failure with systolic dysfunction include all of the following except
questions.explanation: Systolic dysfunction is the commoner pattern of failure, and is caused by ischaemic heart disease, myopathy, or severe volume or pressure overload from valve pathology: it results in a dilated ventricl (increased end diastolic volume) with reduced ejection fraction (giving increased end systolic volume Diastolic dysfunction is reduced ventricular compliance, as seen with extreme myocardial hypertroph in, for example, hypertrophic subaortic stenosis, or longstanding severe hypertension. The hypertrophied, stiffer ventricle requires increased diastolic filling pressure. In this respect, it is similar to systolic dysfunction, though the mechanism is different (A correct). With systolic dysfunction, the failing ventricle needs increased filling pressure to achieve increased end-diastolic volume and move it further up the Starling curve. With diastolic dysfunction, the increased stiffness requires increased filling pressure to approach a normal end-diastolic volume. The hypertrophied muscle has increased performance, so that the ejection fraction is increased.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: A congenital ventricular septal defect would be associated with all except
options: D. possible late right ventricular failure
questions.explanation: Flow through septal defects follows the pressure gradients: therefore, both atrial and ventricular septal defects usually have left-to-right flow unless the pressures are highly abnormal. Cyanosis requires the delivery of deoxygenated blood to the left heart and so to the systemic circulation: ie right-to-left shunts. Left-to-right shunts do not result in cyanosis, though they increase pulmonary blood flow. A late sequel to the increased volume load on the right ventricle and pulmonary circulatio may be attenuation of the pulmonary vasculature, pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure. The murmur of a VSD is pansystolic since it reflects only the pressure profile of the ventricle and not the acceleration of the long, massive, blood column in the aorta, which determines the diamond-shaped systolic murmur of aortic stenosis. All the options are plausible associations, except C, which is therefore the required answer.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Volume overload in a left ventricle with valve pathology will occur with
options: E. combined aortic and mitral insufficiency
questions.explanation: Cardiac output is actually regulated by factors external to the heart, so that the heart meets demands, unless the patient is in cardiogenic shock leading to circulatory failure. Cardiac output must be kept normal, despite changes in valve function. In aortic insufficiency, the stroke volume increases so that the output is kept normal despite part of the stroke volume being lost back into the ventricle during diastole. Likewise, in mitral insufficiency, the volume refluxing back into the atria must be pumped again at the next cycle. Aortic stenosis increases pressure workload, but does not increase volume load; while in mitral stenosis, the left ventricle is protected and the increased pressure is in the left atrium. The answer is option E, with both aortic and mitral insufficiency.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: A loud pericardial rub is consistent with
options: C. an infective or systemic inflammatory process
E. none of the above features
questions.explanation: Pericardial effusions are commonly due to infectious pericarditis (Coxsackie virus, influenza, echoviruses, HIV) or occasionally due to collagen diseases such as SLE (C correct). Because the fluid is often rich in fibrin, it may produce a loud rub, despite having a large volume that prevents contact between the myocardium and the pericardium. Thus, loud rubs are by no means inconsistent with large or even life-threatening effusions. The ECG changes reflect myocardial inflammation and are typically ST depressions and T wave changes, not the Q waves which are seen in full-thickness myocardial infarction.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: A majority of patients with significant pulmonary thromboembolism show
options: C. clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis
questions.explanation: Pulmonary thromboembolism was recently the third most frequent cause of death in the USA. Clinical diagnosis is made difficult by the inconstancy of clinical signs: only a minority of patients present the textbook picture of haemoptysis, friction rub, gallop rhythm, cyanosis, wide fixed split of the second sound and signs of the source of the embolism from deep vein thrombosis in the legs. The majority o patients, however, do have tachycardia and dyspnoea, at least transiently (E True).

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: The procedure and interpretation of the Brodie-Trendelenburg test include all the following except
options: A. the patient reclines with the leg elevated to empty the veins
B. the superficial veins are compressed in the thigh
C. the patient then stands while the veins are observed
D. rapid filling on standing of the superficial veins below the knee during the phase of compression indicates incompetent leg and ankle perforators
E. rapid filling of the long saphenous vein from above on release of the tourniquet indicates deep venous occlusion extending up to the saphenofemoral junction
questions.explanation: he Brodie-Trendelenburg procedure is described correctly except for item E, which is therefore the required answer. Rapid filling from above of the long saphenous vein after removal of pressure from the saphenofemoral junction indicates incompetence of the saphenofemoral junction, rather than of the valves in the lower deep venous system. The Brodie-Trendelenburg test can sometimes be additionally useful in detecting incompetent lower leg and ankle perforators, which indicate severe dysfunction of the venomuscular pump. Duplex-Doppler venous flow studies are now increasingly used to pinpoint incompetent perforators.

questions.topic_label: Cardiovascular Physiology — Dynamics of Blood & Lymph Flow
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Venous pressure in the veins of the foot exhibits all the following properties except
options: A. in all subjects, increases on standing
B. in normal subjects, diminishes on exercise
C. in subjects with varicose veins but competent perforators, fails to diminish on exercise
D. in subjects with incompetence of the perforators and valves of the deep veins, remains elevated during exercise
E. in all subjects, diminishes on elevation of the legs
questions.explanation: The key to understanding the pathology of the venous system of the lower limb is the operation of th veno-muscular pump. Simple physics dictates that the pressures in the veins of the dependent limb will tend to increase in the standing posture by up to the equivalent of a column of blood from ankle t heart - a little over a metre of water, about 100 millimetres of mercury. Pumping the blood up the limb on exercise depends on the competence of the valves in the ankle perforators and the deep veins. Cyclic compression of the deep veins pushes blood up the deep veins during their positive pressure excursions. Competent perforators allow blood from the saphenous system to enter the deep veins during their negative pressure excursions, without allowing that blood back into the superficial veins the next contraction of leg muscles. Even patients with incompetence of the valves in the saphenous system, but competent perforators, experience a fall in venous pressure on walking - though it is not as marked as the fall with competent valves at all levels. Option C describes the behaviour incorrectly, and is therefore the required answer. RESPIRATORY

questions.stem: The following acid-base data pH 7.21 PaCO 20 mmHg HCO 8 2 3 mmol/1 BE -19mmol/1 would be most consistent with
options: A. lobar atelectasis of the lung
E. duodenal ulcer with pyloric obstruction
questions.explanation: The data pattern suggests a partially compensated metabolic acidosis because the hypocapnia is accompanied by a low pH and low bicarbonate together with a large negative base excess. This is not due to atelectasis of the lung, because the low PaCO would not be accompanied by the extreme 2 hypoxaemia needed to produce such a severe metabolic acidosis (A false), nor is it due to anxiety as the pH would be raised in the presence of the hypocapnia (D false). It is not pyloric obstruction (with vomiting) where one would expect acid loss resulting in metabolic alkalosis (E false). Both starvation and septic shock would result in metabolic acidosis, but the former would be mild and compensated with a higher pH and plasma bicarbonate (B false). Therefore this severe acid-base disturbance would be most consistent with the anaerobic metabolism of septic shock (C true).

questions.stem: A patient suffers from a metabolic acidosis due to excessive production of keto-acids. In this state all of the following exist EXCEPT
options: B. decreased PCO2 of the arterial blood
C. increased renal excretion of titratable acid
E. an increased rate of production of bicarbonate
questions.explanation: Little free hydrogen can be excreted in the urine; so in acidosis excess quantities of urinary hydrogen ion secreted are buffered with ammonia and phosphate buffers (A and C false). Free hydrogen ion is buffered by bicarbonate derived from CO2 and H2O to form carbonic anhydrase with dissociation to HCO and H+. The latter is excreted in the tubules in exchange for Na. This process is driven by increased H+ ions (D true) which cause increased rate and depth of respiration to blow off CO2 and decrease the blood pCO2 (E and B false).

questions.stem: Renin secretion is controlled by

statements.text: intrarenal baroreceptors
statements.explanation: Renin is produced in the juxtaglomerular apparatus by stimuli that decrease extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure or increase sympathetic output. The control of renin secretion is achieved by an intrarenal baroreceptor mechanism which causes renin secretion to increase when the intra-arterial pressure at the juxtaglomerular cells is decreased (A true)

statements.explanation: Substance P is a neural transmitter that is liberated in the primary afferent neurons in the brain, the retina and gastrointestinal tract (B false)

statements.explanation: The macula densa cells of the distal + convoluted tubule form the part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus which is sensitive to the NA and CI concentration of the fluid delivered to it, renin secretion being partly controlled by the rate of transport - + of CI and NA across the macula densa cells (C true)

statements.text: glomerular filtration rate
statements.explanation: The glomerular filtrate is governed by the hydrostatic pressure in the afferent arteriole which, of course, affects the juxtaglomerular apparatus. However, the glomerular filtration rate does not control renin secretion (D false)

questions.stem: Which of the following normally has the highest renal clearance?

Inulin is not secreted or reabsorbed in the renal tubules and is excreted as it is filtered (A false) but para-amino hippurate is secreted in the proximal tubules so that it is nearly totally cleared from the plasma by the time the blood leaves the kidney (C true). questions.stem: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle
options: A. is impermeable to sodium ions
B. actively transports the majority of potassium ions
C. actively transports most of the filtered water into the tubule lumen
D. actively transports chloride ions out of the tubule lumen
E. actively transports sodium ions into the tubule lumen
questions.explanation: The loop of Henle is active in the final event for increasing the osmolar concentration of urine. Sodium and chloride ions are transported into the inner medullary interstitium (A and E false; D true). Similarly only 27% of filtered potassium is actively reabsorbed in the loop of Henle, 65% having previously been actively transported in the proximal tubule. D is more appropriate than B in the context of the question.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: The phosphate buffer system plays a major role in H+ buffering in the tubules
statements.explanation: The phosphate buffer system plays a major role in H+ buffering in the renal tubules, since phosphate is poorly reabsorbed and becomes concentrated as water is reabsorbed, making it an effective tubular buffer.

statements.text: the phosphate buffer system has a pK suited to the pH of tubular fluid
statements.explanation: Phosphate's pK of 6.8 is well suited to the pH of tubular fluid (which falls toward about 6.0 as urine is concentrated), allowing it to function near its most effective buffering range, which explains its major buffering role.

statements.text: During acidosis the pH of the glomerular filtrate can fall below 4.5 in the proximal tubule
statements.explanation: Although most H+ secretion occurs in the proximal tubule via the Na+/H+ counter-transporter, the maximum concentration gradient achievable there is only about three-fold, so proximal tubular fluid pH does not fall below about 6.9, not below 4.5; this statement is false.

statements.text: the proximal tubule is the major site for removal of HCO from the filtrate

questions.stem: Regarding the acidification of urine

questions.stem: A 37-year-old patient is noted to be difficult to rouse one hour after a subcutaneous injection of 12.5 mg morphine. Her respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min. Which one of the following statements is most correct?
options: A. No immediate action is required but the amount of morphine she is given next time should be reduced
B. She does not have respiratory depression
C. She may have respiratory depression and should be given supplemental oxygen and 1000 ?g naloxone iv prn
D. She may have respiratory depression and should be given supplemental oxygen and 100 ?g naloxone iv prn
E. She should be given supplemental oxygen and nalorphine
questions.explanation: Respiratory depression from opiate is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with a Sedation Score 3. She requires supplemental oxygen to treat potential hypoxia; and naloxone intravenously as the specific morphine antagonist, in a starting dose of 100 micrograms intravenously to observe the initia effect (D).

statements.explanation: Intracellular lipase is the hormone-sensitive lipase which is confined to adipose tissue and catalyses the breakdown of stored triglyceride to glycerol and fatty acids, the latter being released into the circulation. questions.stem: Which of the following increases blood glucose, mobilises fat from depots and has no effect on protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline increases blood glucose by increasing hepatic glycogenolysis and increases circulating free fatty acids (C true). Glucagon has similar effects but also increases gluconeogenesis from available amino acids (B false). Cortisol increases protein catabolism and tends to increase blood glucose levels (D false). Growth hormone stimulates protein synthesis, increases hepatic glucose production and elevates free fatty levels in plasma (E false). Insulin, on the other hand, lowers blood glucose levels, increases protein synthesis and increases triglyceride deposition in adipose tissue (A false).

questions.stem: The most clinically useful form of nutritional assessment related to body weight is:
options: A. Absolute weight measured on an accurate set of scales.
C. Body mass index (BMI: weight divided by the square of height).
D. A history of unintentional weight loss greater than 10% over the preceeding 6 months.
E. Body composition measurement using neutron activation.
questions.explanation: Body weight can be compared with an "ideal" or "desirable" weight, or assessment of body mass index can be used to determine both undernutrition and overnutrition. However, measurement of body weight in sick patients is confounded by changes in body water because of dehydration, oedema, and ascites. Furthermore, a person who starts at the upper end of the normal range may be classified as "normal" despite considerable changes in the measured value. Dietary recall histories lack reliability and are associated with poor compliance from those who are seriously ill. Unintentional weight loss greater than 10% over the previous six months is a good prognosticator of clinical outcome. However, it can be difficult to determine true weight loss because of errors in recall. It has been estimated that one-third of patients with weight loss would be missed and one-quarter of weight-stable patients would be diagnosed as having lost weight when weight loss is based on patient recall. So, although it is the most clinically useful of the measurements that have been listed, it is a far from perfect measure of nutritional status. Formal measures of body composition, such as neutron activation, provide accurate and precise information, but a detailed understanding of the body's muscle, fat, and water content is more relevant to clinical research than it is to clinical practice.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about anthropometric measurements, such as triceps skinfold thickness and midarm circumference, best describes their clinical role:
options: A. Simple measurements that are highly reliable.
B. Values below the 5th percentile are associated with a poor clinical outcome.
C. Simple measurements that lack reliability, but are very precise.
D. Such measures cannot be used to estimate muscle mass.
E. Useful ward-based tests that should be employed by nutrition support teams.
questions.explanation: Anthropometry uses simple measurements of body thicknesses to estimate fat and lean tissue mass. Triceps and subscapular skinfold thicknesses provide an index of body fat; and midarm muscle circumference provides a measure of muscle mass. Interpretation of the data may be limited by interobserver variability, age, and hydration status. Nevertheless, markedly abnormal values, below the 5th percentile, are often associated with poor clinical outcome. However, such patients usually look thin and wasted from the foot of the bed. Anthropometry is most appropriate when evaluating groups rather than individuals and starved young populations rather than sick and elderly patients. Hence, they offer a low technology approach to the measurement of body composition that is most applicable to epidemiological surveys of starving third-world populations. It might be more appropriate to measure muscle function rather than muscle bulk. Muscle function testing represents a new approach for evaluating the adequacy of nutrient intake and entifying patients who are at increased risk for complications. Muscle function tests include measuring grip strength, respiratory muscle strength, and the response of specific muscles to electrical stimulation. Some initial studies have suggested that they are more accurate than other measures of nutritional status. It is unknown whether restoring muscle function with nutritional therapy improves clinical outcome. THYROID

questions.stem: Concerning the ovary

statements.text: luteinising hormone stimulates the secretion of oestrogen from the theca interna
statements.explanation: and also secrete oestrogens under the stimulus of LH (1 True)

statements.text: follicle-stimulating hormone regulates the theca interna
statements.explanation: Both follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH) are secreted by the anterior pituitary in response to stimulation of the pituitary by gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secreted by the hypothalamus. Ovarian function is entirely dependent on stimulation by FSH/LH. FSH, in particular, stimulates the accelerated growth of 6-12 primary follicles with rapid proliferation of granulosa cells as well as a second class of cells that form theca interna and externa. As its name suggests the development of the primary follicle to vesicular follicle is due to FSH. Both granulosa cells and theca interna cells secrete oestrogens. Granulosa cells initially have FSH receptors but later develop LH receptors. Theca interna cells have LH receptors, not FSH (2 False)

statements.text: plasma oestrogen level peaks about day 8 of a 28-day menstrual cycle
statements.explanation: LH is needed for the final development of the follicle, as well as ovulation. There is a rapid rise of both LH & FSH in the hours before ovulation. LH then seems to convert the granulosa and theca interna cells into a more progesterone-secreting type of cell. The rise and fall of the various hormones are seen subsequently in Figures 4 and 5. Plasma oestrogen levels peak near ovulation in midcycle (3 False)

statements.text: during the first trimester of pregnancy, bilateral oophorectomy may be followed by abortion
statements.explanation: The progesterone secreted by ovarian corpus luteum in the second half of the menstrual cycle prepares a receptive endometrium for the fertilised ovum (Figures 4 and 5). After implantation, ongoing nutrition of this conceptus is dependent on corpus luteum secretion of progesterone, oestrogen and relaxin. After about six weeks the placenta is able to produce enough oestrogen and progesterone to maintain pregnancy. Oophorectomy before the sixth week will thus lead to abortion (4 True)

When considering abnormal menstrual loss it is best to remember that: 1 'menorrhagia' is excessive bleeding in regular cycles and tends to have a local cause in uterine fibroids, or faulty clotting. 2 'polymenorrhea' are periods that are too frequent, due usually to a disturbance of the hormones of the pituitary/ovarian axis (2 False)

statements.text: stress can upset the menstrual cycle
statements.explanation: 3 'polymenorrhagia' is the condition of periods that are both too heavy and too frequent, usually due to a combination of the above causes. Alterations to the menstrual cycle can be due to emotional and traumatic factors acting on neuro- endocrine effector pathways (3 True)

questions.stem: Concerning post-menopausal vaginal bleeding

statements.text: exogenous oestrogens are a possible cause
statements.explanation: Exogenous oestrogens influence the endometrial lining causing proliferation of the endometrial stroma and glandular proliferation with shedding of this thickened layer is likely with any drop in the level of oestrogen. Such 'post-menopausal' bleeding is a common effect of female 'hormone replacement therapy' (HRT) (1 True)

statements.text: uterine cancer needs to be ruled out
statements.explanation: Uterine cancer is a very important diagnosis and a common cause of post-menopausal bleeding (2 True)

statements.text: urethral caruncle is very rarely a factor
statements.explanation: About 25% of post-menopausal bleeding is due to a genital malignancy. A urethral caruncle is an inflammatory lesion that occurs (quite commonly) at the external urethral meatus, usually in elderly women. It is a highly vascular lesion with young connective tissue and a variably present epithelial covering of transitional or squamous cells. It is equally important to examine the external genitalia thoroughly as cancer or infection externally can be interpreted as blood of vaginal origin. Caruncle is an important and relatively frequent cause of vaginal bleeding (3 False)

statements.text: post-menopausal vaginal bleeding can be caused by colon cancer
statements.explanation: Due to the relatively thin 'window' of the posterior vaginal fornix it is possible, although unusual, for an abdominal cancer to grow through into the vagina to cause bleeding (4 True)

statements.explanation: Normal spermatogenesis requires both FSH and adequate intratesticular testosterone (via LH-stimulated Leydig cells), not FSH alone, so this statement is false.

statements.text: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin which has a negative feedback effect on the anterior pituitary
statements.explanation: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which exerts negative feedback on FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary.

statements.text: testosterone from Leydig cells inhibits the release of F.S.H. from the anterior pituitary
statements.explanation: Testosterone's negative feedback acts mainly on LH secretion (via the hypothalamus and pituitary) to stabilise testosterone levels, rather than primarily inhibiting FSH release, so this statement is false.

statements.text: testosterone inhibits luteinising hormone secretion at the level of the hypothalamus
statements.explanation: Testosterone inhibits luteinising hormone secretion mainly at the hypothalamic level, by suppressing GnRH release, which in turn reduces pituitary LH output.

questions.stem: Concerning renal trauma

statements.text: general resuscitation measures are the first priority in any multi-trauma case
CT scan is the imaging modality of choice in the acute phase
statements.explanation: True. Remember your A B Cs (as per EMST). CT scanning allows assessment of renal perfusion; the presence and function of the contralateral kidney; the extent, if any, of perirenal haematoma; and the presence or absence of urinary extravasation (2 True)

statements.text: surgical exploration is required for all cases of renal trauma requiring blood transfusion
statements.explanation: If CT scans are not available intravenous pyelography may be used but this study is inadequate in 20% of cases. In the presence of continued or severe haemorrhage, arteriography may be helpful to elucidate the site of arterial bleeding and the presence or absence of arteriovenous malformation. Surgical exploration and repair or nephrectomy may be necessary in the presence of continued severe haemorrhage. Patients who respond to blood transfusion and remain stable do not necessaril require exploration. Surgery will more often be required for assessment and treatment of other intra- abdominal injuries include damage to spleen, duodenum and bowel (3 False)

statements.text: hypertension can occur in the long term after conservative management of renal trauma
statements.explanation: Causes of hypertension include: • The 'Page' kidney with increased pressure due to a chronic subcapsular haematoma causing release of renin. • Renal artery stenosis/thrombosis. • A-V fistula (4 True)

statements.text: the flank approach is ideal for isolated renal injuries
statements.explanation: Approach should be from a midline vertical laparotomy incision to obtain best exposure and vascular control when dealing with renal trauma (5 False)

statements.text: penetrating renal injuries almost invariably require exploration

questions.explanation: . Penetrating renal trauma (bullets and stab injury) will commonly be associated with injuries to other intra-abdominal and thoracic viscera. Surgical exploration will almost invariably be necessary to repair other structures and to perform drainage. High powered shotgun injuries will be associated with more widespread tissue destruction and necrosis requiring, at times, extensive debridement and drainage (6 True).

questions.stem: A previously fit 55 year old man has undergone an emergency right hemicolectomy for a perforated caecal carcinoma. On review 24 hours after the operation you note the following on his fluid balance sheet - intravenous input 2L, nasogastric aspirate 2L, drain losses 700 ml, urine output 500 ml. Biochemistry shows Na+ 135 mmol/L, K+ 3.0 mmol/L, Cl- 100 mmol/L, HC03- 27 mmol/L. Which of the fluid balance regimens below would you order for the next 24 hr period?
options: A. 2L N. saline + 3L dextrose 5% + 50 mmol KCl
B. 2L N. saline + 1L dextrose 5% + 50 mmol KCl
C. 1L N. saline + 3L dextrose 5% + 100 mmol KCl
D. 3L N. saline + 2L dextrose 5% + 100 mmol KCl
E. 1L N. saline + 1L dextrose 5% + 100 mmol KCl
questions.explanation: He has a total of 3200 ml sensible loss in the previous 24 hours, compared to a 2000 ml intake; and his urine output has only been 500 ml in that 24 hours. He is hypokalaemic. He is likely to be ‘saline’ depleted; and should have 5000 ml of fluid ordered in the next 24 hours to allow for this, with additional saline for ECF losses and both basal and additional potassium intake. D is thus the best combination.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Apoptosis

statements.text: causes cell death by enzyme-induced membrane injury
statements.explanation: Apoptosis causes cell death via activation of calcium-sensitive endogenous endonuclease, not enzyme-induced membrane injury, so this statement is false.

statements.text: occurs in prostatic epithelial cells following castration
statements.explanation: Withdrawal of the relevant hormone (as occurs after castration) induces apoptosis in hormone-dependent prostatic epithelial cells.

statements.text: is the common mechanism of cancer cell death following chemotherapy
statements.explanation: Chemotherapy appropriate to the cancer characteristically induces apoptosis in susceptible tumour cells, making it a common mechanism of cancer cell death after treatment.

statements.text: results in a predominantly eosinophil leukocyte inflammatory reaction
statements.explanation: Apoptotic cell death does not typically provoke an inflammatory reaction (eosinophilic or otherwise) unless it is extensive, such as in massive chemically-induced tumour lysis, so this statement is false.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Cell Injury & Death & Adaptation
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Apoptosis

statements.text: has important regulatory influence on normal cell population
statements.explanation: Apoptosis has an important regulatory role in maintaining normal cell populations as part of normal physiological turnover.

statements.text: is the mechanism causing menopausal ovarian follicle atresia
statements.explanation: Apoptosis is the mechanism causing menopausal ovarian follicle atresia, reflecting its normal physiological role in tissue regulation.

statements.text: commonly causes polymorphonuclear leukocyte reaction
statements.explanation: Apoptotic cell death does not provoke a polymorphonuclear leukocyte (inflammatory) reaction; the main cellular response is phagocytosis of apoptotic bodies by adjacent cells, so this statement is false.

statements.text: induces cell death through lysosomal enzyme activation
statements.explanation: Apoptosis induces cell death via activation of endogenous endonuclease causing DNA denaturation, not via lysosomal enzyme activation, so this statement is false.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Apoptosis

statements.text: mediates development of endothelial injury in Gram-negative sepsis
statements.explanation: Endothelial injury in Gram-negative sepsis is thought to be mediated by IL-1/TNF rather than apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: results from plasma membrane ‘ionic pump’ failure
statements.explanation: Ionic pump failure with resulting cell swelling is typically induced by hypoxic injury, not apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: mediates the vascular injury causing ‘fibrinoid’ necrosis
statements.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis is usually an expression of the Arthus (immune complex) reaction rather than apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: is a major mechanism of cell injury in graft-versus-host reactions
statements.explanation: Graft-versus-host reactions are Tc-lymphocyte-mediated, and as with transplant allograft rejection and some viral infections, cell death is mediated by host endonuclease activation, i.e. apoptosis.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Apoptosis

statements.text: is a determinant of growth rate of many cancers
statements.explanation: Genes regulating apoptosis, such as bcl-2 (which inhibits apoptosis) and p53 (which normally promotes apoptosis in damaged cells), influence cancer growth rates, making apoptosis a real determinant of tumour growth kinetics.

statements.text: is a major cause of shock in Gram-negative bacteraemia
statements.explanation: Mediation of shock in Gram-negative bacteraemia is complex and multifactorial, involving many acute inflammatory mediators, with apoptosis not appearing to play a significant role, so this statement is false.

statements.text: will result from carbon tetrachloride (CCI) cell poisoning 4
statements.explanation: Carbon tetrachloride poisoning is membrane-damaging and, when severe enough to cause cell death, induces necrosis rather than apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: is a form of programmed cell destruction in normal body processes
statements.explanation: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death that plays a major role in normal body processes and regulation of cell populations.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Cell Injury & Death & Adaptation
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Apoptosis is cell death which

statements.text: is caused by activation of endogenous endonuclease
statements.explanation: Apoptosis is mediated by activation of endogenous endonuclease, triggered through pathways such as p53 activation.

statements.text: results in ‘haematoxylin body’ formation in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
statements.explanation: The haematoxylin body seen in SLE is produced by anti-DNA antibody coating a naked (usually lymphocyte) nucleus followed by its phagocytosis, a different mechanism from apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: may result from virus-induced Tc cytotoxic effect
statements.explanation: Apoptosis may result from a virus-induced cytotoxic T lymphocyte (Tc) effect, where Tc cells interact with the virion-MHC I complex on the surface of infected cells, triggering endonuclease-mediated death.

statements.text: induces a brisk acute inflammatory reaction
statements.explanation: Apoptosis does not provoke a brisk acute inflammatory reaction; it is sometimes described as 'death without fuss', so this statement is false.

questions.stem: Apoptosis is the major mechanism causing

statements.text: hepatocyte death in acute viral hepatitis
statements.explanation: Cell death in many viral infections, such as acute viral hepatitis, occurs via apoptosis, producing the Councilman body surrounded by lymphocytes that induced the cell death.

statements.text: cell death due to chemical poisons
statements.explanation: Severe chemical poisoning typically causes cell necrosis with the full inflammatory consequences, rather than apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: renal tubule cell death in cell-mediated transplant rejection
statements.explanation: Lymphocyte (Tc)-mediated cell death of similar pathogenesis to viral infection is also the mechanism of renal tubule cell death in acute, cell-mediated transplant rejection.

statements.text: cancer cell death induced by radiotherapy
statements.explanation: Radiotherapy (like therapeutic-dose chemotherapy) induces apoptosis in susceptible cancer cells, provided the injury is not too severe to instead cause necrosis.

statements.explanation: Menopausal ovarian follicle atrophy is a classic example of apoptosis induced by hormone withdrawal.

statements.explanation: Salivary gland atrophy following duct obstruction is an example of pressure-induced apoptosis.

statements.text: prostatic epithelial cells following castration
statements.explanation: Prostatic epithelial cell death following castration is a classic example of apoptosis induced by hormone (androgen) withdrawal.

statements.text: lactating breast epithelium during weaning
statements.explanation: Involution of lactating breast epithelium during weaning is another example of apoptosis induced by hormone withdrawal, occurring without an inflammatory reaction.

questions.stem: Important mechanisms which mediate cell death by apoptosis include

statements.text: lysosomal enzyme release and activation
statements.explanation: Lysosomal enzyme release and activation is associated with membrane injury (necrosis), not the primary DNA attack of apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: denaturation of cell and cytoplasmic organelles
statements.explanation: Denaturation of cell and cytoplasmic organelles reflects primary membrane injury seen in necrosis, not the DNA-directed process of apoptosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: Ca2+-dependent, endonuclease-induced DNA denaturation
statements.explanation: Apoptosis involves a primary attack on cell DNA via Ca2+-dependent endonuclease activation, which is the central mechanism mediating apoptotic death.

statements.text: endogenous activation of oxidising free radicals
statements.explanation: Endogenous oxidising free radical activation is linked to membrane injury (necrosis via cell oxidase systems), not apoptosis, so this statement is false.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Cell Injury & Death & Adaptation
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Necrosis

statements.text: causes rapid development of intracellular alkalosis
statements.explanation: The early response to lethal cell damage is increased glycolysis (from ATP decrease) causing cytoplasmic acidosis, not alkalosis, so this statement is false; alkalosis may only occur as a late finding in far-advanced cell derangement.

statements.text: is often haemorrhagic if blood flow is rapidly restored following lethal ischaemia (‘reperfusion’)
statements.explanation: Haemorrhagic infarction is almost the rule with rapid reperfusion following lethal ischaemia, as occurs spontaneously (e.g. in the brain after embolic lysis) or with thrombolytic therapy.

statements.text: never occurs as a result of T-lymphocyte-mediated reactions
statements.explanation: Many cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (Tc) responses do result in necrosis-associated tissue reactions (such as brisk TH2 reactions like the Mantoux reaction), so the claim that necrosis never occurs from T-lymphocyte-mediated reactions is false.

statements.text: in brain tissue does not elicit an acute inflammatory response
statements.explanation: Necrosis always elicits an acute inflammatory reaction in all tissues, including brain, so the claim that it does not in brain tissue is false.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Cell Injury & Death & Adaptation
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Necrosis

statements.text: always induces an acute inflammatory reaction
statements.explanation: Necrosis always induces an acute inflammatory reaction, whether mild or marked, since it is always a pathological process.

statements.text: on occasion serves an essentially physiological function
statements.explanation: Necrosis is always pathological and does not serve a physiological function (unlike apoptosis), so this statement is false.

statements.text: usually results in rapid depletion of cytoplasmic glycogen
statements.explanation: Interference with cellular oxygen supply usually results in rapid glycolysis with attendant lactate accumulation, which rapidly depletes cytoplasmic glycogen.

statements.text: has its usual common pathway of causation through membrane damage
statements.explanation: The current evidence strongly favours cell membrane injury (plasma or mitochondrial) as the final common pathway leading to cell death in necrosis, regardless of the inciting cause.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Cell Injury & Death & Adaptation
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Necrosis

statements.text: commonly induces a moderate lymphocytic infiltration
statements.explanation: Necrosis always induces an acute inflammatory response first, never a lymphocytic one (even if the underlying cause is Tc-lymphocyte mediated), so this statement is false.

statements.text: is not caused by any of the ‘reactive’ body processes (immune, inflammatory, etc)
statements.explanation: Immune and acute inflammatory reactions can and commonly do cause tissue necrosis, so the claim that necrosis is never caused by reactive body processes is false.

statements.text: if solid and structureless (‘caseous’), is diagnostic of tuberculosis
statements.explanation: Caseous (solid, structureless) necrosis occurs in many infective diseases and some non-infective conditions like Wegener's granulomatosis, not exclusively tuberculosis, so this statement is false.

statements.text: may form a nidus for deposition of calcium salts
statements.explanation: Calcium deposition is common within necrotic tissue, such as in comedo carcinoma or tuberculous foci, so necrosis may indeed form a nidus for calcium salt deposition.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Cell Injury & Death & Adaptation
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Necrosis

statements.text: can be confidently diagnosed if one observes nuclear pyknosis
statements.explanation: Nuclear pyknosis (along with karyolysis and karyorrhexis) is one of the 'hard' confirmatory signs of cell death by necrosis.

statements.text: usually rapidly causes cytoplasmic acidosis
statements.explanation: Failure of aerobic metabolism plus activation of glycolytic enzyme systems (particularly with hypoxic cell death) rapidly causes cytoplasmic acidosis in necrosis.

statements.text: is pathogenetically different in neurones and myocardial cells
statements.explanation: Necrosis is pathogenetically the same fundamental process regardless of cell type (neurones or myocardial cells); it is not pathogenetically different between them, so this statement is false.

statements.text: is most commonly induced by nuclear DNA damage
statements.explanation: Necrosis is most commonly induced by membrane damage and metabolic failure, not primarily by nuclear DNA damage; DNA damage is instead the common trigger for apoptosis, so this statement is false.

questions.explanation: See individual statement explanations above.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: The eventual zone of tissue necrosis caused by arterial occlusion is larger if ischaemic tissue is quickly reperfused
statements.explanation: Although rapid reperfusion does cause additional local oxygen free radical injury, the eventual zone of necrosis is in fact significantly smaller with early reperfusion than if the occlusion were left untreated (which is why early thrombolysis is used clinically), so this statement is false.

statements.text: oxygen free radicals, which can cause cell injury, are generate locally in ischaemic tissues following rapid reperfusion.
statements.explanation: Oxygen free radicals are indeed generated locally in reperfused ischaemic tissue, via mechanisms including infiltrating polymorphs, incomplete mitochondrial oxygen reduction, and endothelial xanthine oxidase activity, causing genuine reperfusion injury even though overall infarct size is still reduced by early reperfusion.

questions.stem: Induction of free radicals, with resultant cell injury, occurs as a result of

statements.text: Tc-lymphocyte immune reactions
statements.explanation: Tc-lymphocyte immune reactions induce cell death via apoptosis (endonuclease activation), not via free radical generation, so this statement is false.

statements.text: cyanide poisoning
statements.explanation: Cyanide poisoning acts by denaturing cytochrome oxidase, blocking electron transfer and aerobic metabolism, rather than by generating free radicals, so this statement is false.

statements.text: acute inflammation
statements.explanation: Toxic oxygen radicals are generated in phagocytic cells during acute inflammation, including in 'reverse phagocytosis' situations, making this a genuine cause of free radical-induced injury.

statements.text: carbon tetrachloride (CCI) poisoning 4
statements.explanation: Carbon tetrachloride supplies the initial free radical and then autocatalytically induces further 'secondary' free radicals, causing cell injury.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: It is accepted that cell membrane damage is a central factor in the pathogenesis of irreversible cell injury from many causes
statements.explanation: Cell membrane damage is accepted as a central factor in the pathogenesis of irreversible cell injury across many different causes of injury.

statements.text: loss of (membrane-based) regulation of cell volume and ionic gradients, plus cell membrane ultrastructural defects, are found in the earliest stages of irreversible injury.
statements.explanation: Loss of membrane-based regulation of cell volume and ionic gradients, together with membrane ultrastructural defects, are found at the earliest stages of irreversible injury, supporting membrane damage as the central mechanism (with calcium influx then activating phospholipases, proteases, ATPases and endonucleases that cause further injury).

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Cytoplasmic pH falls in cells lethally injured due to hypoxia
statements.explanation: Cytoplasmic pH does fall in cells lethally injured by hypoxia, due to loss of ATP and accumulation of AMP driving increased anaerobic glycolysis and lactate accumulation.

statements.text: activation of lysosomal enzymes during cell necrosis causes the early pH fall in lethal hypoxic cell injury.
statements.explanation: Lysosomal enzyme activation occurs in the later, more complex stages of cell necrosis and typically raises rather than lowers pH; it does not explain the well-recognised early pH fall seen in hypoxic cell injury, so this statement is false.

questions.stem: Morphological features indicating cell death include each of the following except
options: A. nuclear shrinkage and chromatin condensation
D. rupture of cell plasma membrane
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial swelling (‘high amplitude swelling’) is a good indicator of very significant cell injury, but not of cell death. Calcification of mitochondria is a death knell for the cell and indicates that the organelle is non-functional and more significantly, that cell membrane rupture has occurred allowing sufficient change in the electrolyte gradient for mitochondrial calcification to occur.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Of the following cellular changes which are possible sequelae of hypoxia, the one which occurs last is
options: B. impaired respiration and ATP formation
D. impaired synthesis of protein in membrane
E. change from aerobic to anaerobic glycolysis
questions.explanation: This question lists a series of degenerative changes in the cell. Options B to E represent a sequence of progressively more severe cytoplasmic damage, in which the earliest change is described in Optio B and the most severe abnormality in Option E. If these changes are to occur the cell must be alive. Karyolysis (Option A) is nuclear dissolution and thus characterises cell death. Clearly the cytoplasmic changes listed in B to E could not occur if the cell were dead. Of the changes listed karyolysis is the last to occur (A true).

statements.explanation: Renal tubule cells are 'acid-producing' tissue and are a prime site for metastatic calcium phosphate deposition during states of hypercalcaemia.

statements.explanation: Alveolar walls of the lung are similarly 'acid-producing' tissue and a classic site for metastatic calcification in hypercalcaemia.

statements.explanation: Acute leukaemia similarly causes hypercalcaemia via bone resorption, so alveolar wall calcification here is metastatic rather than dystrophic, making this statement false.

statements.explanation: Psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid carcinoma represent calcification occurring within abnormal tumour connective tissue, a classic example of dystrophic calcification.

statements.explanation: Calcification of comedo breast carcinoma occurs within necrotic tumour tissue, another classic example of dystrophic calcification.

statements.explanation: Leukotriene B4 is produced via the lipoxygenase pathway from arachidonic acid in cell membrane phospholipid, synthesised on demand by stimulated cells.

statements.text: Interleukin- (IL-) 2 2
statements.explanation: Interleukin-2 production is particularly the province of activated CD4+ T cells providing 'help', synthesised on demand.

questions.stem: Chemicals activated during/following tissue injury which normally circulate as inactive plasma precursors include

statements.text: platelet activating factor
statements.explanation: Platelet activating factor is stored in granules within some cells and manufactured on demand by others, rather than circulating as an inactive plasma precursor that is then activated, so this statement is false.

statements.text: major basic protein
statements.explanation: Major basic protein is a preformed product of eosinophil granules rather than an inactive circulating plasma precursor, so this statement is false.

statements.text: C3b opsinic factor
statements.explanation: C3b opsonic factor arises from cleavage activation of complement component C3, which does normally circulate as an inactive plasma precursor.

statements.text: plasmin
statements.explanation: Plasmin is generated from its inactive plasma precursor plasminogen via contact activation, fitting the description of an inactive circulating precursor that becomes activated during tissue injury.

statements.text: cytokines
statements.explanation: Fibroblast proliferation and migration during wound healing is largely under the control of growth-promoting and growth-controlling cytokines.

statements.text: expression of adhesion molecules on endothelial cells
statements.explanation: Endothelial adhesion molecules (members of the immunoglobulin family) have no known direct influence on fibroblast activity, so this statement is false.

statements.text: leukotrienes
statements.explanation: Leukotrienes are cell membrane phospholipid derivatives with no known direct effect on fibroblast proliferation or migration, so this statement is false.

statements.text: platelet activating factor (PAF)
statements.explanation: Platelet activating factor, another membrane phospholipid derivative, similarly has no known direct effect on fibroblast proliferation or migration, so this statement is false.

statements.text: gamma interferon
statements.explanation: Gamma-interferon has no direct effect on endothelial cells or venular permeability, so this statement is false.

statements.text: bradykinin
statements.explanation: Bradykinin is a classic mediator that increases venular permeability during acute inflammation.

statements.explanation: Intact endothelium secretes a plasminogen activator (tPA) promoting fibrinolysis, rather than a tPA inhibitor; tPA inhibitor release is more associated with the injured/procoagulant endothelial phenotype, so this statement is false.

statements.text: prostacyclin (PGI2)
statements.explanation: Intact endothelium secretes prostacyclin (PGI2), a powerful vasodilator and platelet inhibitor, as part of its overall anticoagulant, antiplatelet function.

questions.explanation: The two chemoattractants for granulocytes shown are C5a and LTB4. Of the two, LTB4 is generally stated to be the most powerful naturally occurring in inflammation. statements.explanation: Adhesion molecules expressed on endothelial cells (such as the immunoglobulin-family ICAM-1, induced by mediators like IL-1 and TNF) directly mediate leukocyte adhesion (pavementing).

statements.text: adhesion molecules expressed on leukocytes
statements.explanation: Adhesion molecules expressed on leukocytes (selectins and integrins, whose activity is stimulated by mediators like histamine, thrombin and chemotactic agents) directly mediate pavementing together with the endothelial adhesion molecules.

questions.stem: The most powerful action of granulocytes in killing pyogenic bacteria is
questions.explanation: The production of hypochlorite (OHCl) by this enzyme system results in the most powerful bactericid effect against pygenic bacteria. MPO-deficient leukocytes are capable of killing bacteria (albeit more slowly), by virtue of the other oxygen-dependent enzyme systems. Individuals who cannot generate the superoxide radical suffer a major disorder of bacterial killing, chronic granulomatous disease (usually an X-linked disorder).

questions.stem: Free radical derivatives, produced by phagocytes during acute inflammation, kill bacteria and damage host tissues. They include

statements.text: n-acetyl muramidase (lysozyme)
statements.explanation: Lysozyme (n-acetyl muramidase) is a lysosomal enzyme, not an oxygen-derived free radical, so this statement is false.

statements.text: hypochlorite ion
statements.explanation: Hypochlorite ion is generated through the myeloperoxidase-halide system from superoxide-derived precursors, making it a genuine oxygen-derived free radical product.

statements.text: hydrogen peroxide
statements.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is generated from superoxide via the NADPH oxidative system, making it a genuine oxygen-derived free radical product that kills bacteria and damages host tissue.

statements.text: major basic protein
statements.explanation: Major basic protein is a preformed lysosomal/granule product of eosinophils, not an oxygen-derived free radical, so this statement is false.

questions.stem: Induction of free radicals, with resultant cell injury, occurs as a result of

statements.text: cysteine and methionine-containing ‘remedies’
statements.explanation: Cysteine and methionine are antioxidant amino acids and are therefore protective rather than free-radical-inducing, so this statement is false.

statements.text: paracetamol (acetaminophen) poisoning
statements.explanation: Paracetamol is metabolised in the liver to a toxic free radical product, normally detoxified by reduced glutathione, but this system can be overwhelmed in overdose, causing free radical-induced cell injury.

statements.text: prolonged positive pressure ventilation at FIO of 1.0 2
statements.explanation: Raising the inspired oxygen fraction to 1.0 during prolonged positive pressure ventilation intensifies (by mass action) formation of reactive oxygen species, which can damage lung pneumocytes and endothelial cells, contributing to ARDS.

statements.text: immune complex-induced PMN chemotaxis in acute glomerulonephritis
statements.explanation: In acute glomerulonephritis, immune complex-induced PMN chemotaxis leads to PMN exocytosis of toxic oxygen radicals and enzymes that directly cause tissue damage.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Protection from free radical-induced cell injury is afforded by

statements.text: cytochrome enzyme system
statements.explanation: The cytochrome enzyme system is concerned with electron transfer in aerobic metabolism and has no protective or detoxifying action against free radicals, so this statement is false.

statements.text: superoxide dismutase enzyme system
statements.explanation: Superoxide dismutase converts (dismutes) superoxide radicals into less reactive species, providing protection from free radical injury.

statements.text: catalase enzyme system
statements.explanation: Catalase metabolises hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, providing protection from free radical injury.

statements.text: glycolytic (Embden-Meyerhof) pathway enzymes
statements.explanation: Glycolytic (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) enzymes are concerned with anaerobic glycolysis and have no protective or detoxifying action against free radicals, so this statement is false.

statements.explanation: Alpha-interferon has no opsonic activity, so it does not stimulate opsonised phagocytosis, making this statement false.

statements.text: IL-8
statements.explanation: IL-8 is chemotactic rather than opsonic, so it does not stimulate opsonised phagocytosis, making this statement false.

statements.text: immunoglobulin
statements.explanation: Immunoglobulin (its Fc fragment) is one of the two major opsonins, recognised by Fc receptors (FcγR) on phagocytes to stimulate phagocytosis.

statements.text: C3b and fibronectin
statements.explanation: C3b is the major opsonic fragment of complement, and together with fibronectin (binding via complement receptor 3) stimulates phagocytic engulfment of opsonised bacteria.

questions.stem: Resolution of inflammation, with regeneration, leads to restoration of normal structure and function following

statements.text: pneumococcal pneumonia
statements.explanation: In pneumococcal pneumonia, the alveolar basement membrane is not destroyed despite pneumocyte injury, allowing regenerating cells to migrate along the intact framework and restore normal lung structure and function.

statements.text: uncomplicated healing of a sutured surgical incision
statements.explanation: Despite careful suturing, a surgical skin incision always heals with some degree of scarring and dermal appendages do not regenerate, so this does not represent complete restoration of normal structure, making this statement false.

statements.text: pulmonary infarct
statements.explanation: Basement membrane does not survive pulmonary infarction, so healing occurs by scarring rather than true regeneration, making this statement false.

statements.text: paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis
statements.explanation: In paracetamol-induced hepatic necrosis, the basement membrane framework of the liver typically survives, allowing hepatocytes to regenerate along it and restore normal architecture.

questions.stem: Resolution of inflammation and regeneration lead to complete restoration of normal structure and function following healing of

statements.text: renal papillary necrosis
statements.explanation: Renal papillary necrosis destroys the tissue's structural framework entirely, so healing occurs by scarring rather than complete restoration, making this statement false.

statements.text: acute viral hepatitis
statements.explanation: In acute viral hepatitis, cell death occurs predominantly by apoptosis (not necrosis), preserving the basement membrane framework, allowing hepatocytes to regenerate and restore normal structure.

statements.text: hypovolaemic acute renal tubular necrosis
statements.explanation: In hypovolaemic acute renal tubular necrosis, the tubular basement membrane framework typically survives, allowing tubular cells to regenerate along it, with complete recovery of renal structure and function if no complications such as infection occur.

statements.text: liver abscess
statements.explanation: A liver abscess destroys the tissue's structural framework entirely, so healing occurs by scarring rather than complete restoration, making this statement false.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements applies most correctly to synergistic gangrene (chronic progressive bacterial gangrene)?

B. The presence of crepitus confirms clostridial infection
C. The overall mortality rate is about 10%

questions.explanation: Synergistic gangrene occurs in debilitated patients and has a significant mortality of around 10% (C). Crepitus is not usually an early sign and if present, does not confirm clostridial infection. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is adjunctive to surgery, and Clostridium perfringens is not the common organism.

questions.stem: Principles to be followed in the treatment of tetanus include

statements.text: surgical excision of the wound which is left open
statements.explanation: Tetanus is attributed to the anaerobic spore former, Clostridium tetani. Spores in the environment enter cutaneous wounds, and if conditions for germination and growth of the microbe occur - eg necrotic devitalised tissue, anaerobic conditions - the tetanus exotoxin is produced and liberated. This is a neurotoxin which has been referred to as tetanospasmin. Prevention of such infections, which may follow apparently minor skin trauma, therefore, relies on preventing conditions suitable for the growth of the anaerobe. Dead tissue should be excised from wounds which should be left open, ie aerobic (A true)

statements.text: administration of penicillin intravenously
statements.explanation: Treatment consists of high doses of penicillin (B true)

statements.text: administration of human hyperimmune globulin intramuscularly
statements.explanation: NB. IV for clinical (active) desease, but in prophylaxis/prevention give IM (C true)

statements.text: sedation of the patient and respiratory support
statements.explanation: in an attempt to convey some degree of passive immunity to the toxin. The main effect of the toxin is muscle hyperirritability. The toxin blocks inhibitory neurones in the CNS so that stimulatory signals remain unopposed and muscles, including those in the jaw and respiratory system, are constantly stimulated (D true)

questions.stem: In viral hepatitis A, the main clinical effects are due to damage to hepatocytes, caused by
options: A. competitive cell receptor blockade by viral capsid
B. subversion of cell metabolism to virus production
C. inactivation of cyclic-AMP by lymphokines
questions.explanation: The clinical manifestations of hepatitis (A, B, C, etc) are insignificant during the prodromal phase while an immune response is being mounted. Following the immune reaction, the main event is the Tc-mediated destruction of infected hepatocytes (virus-MHC-I/Tc interaction). There may also be some effects of immune complex deposition with the usual common manifestations in skin, joints etc. as the free virus gets ‘mopped up’ by the immunoglobulin which is manufactured by plasma cells, synchronous with T cell production.
