questions.stem: Surgical-site infection rates are increased

statements.text: in the presence of obesity
statements.explanation: Surgical-site infection rates are increased in the presence of obesity, alongside factors like contamination level, operation duration and patient comorbidities.

statements.text: when the skin is left unshaved
statements.explanation: Skin shaving (as opposed to clipping) increases local microbial growth and trauma, raising rather than lowering subsequent wound infection rates, so the claim that leaving skin unshaved increases infection is false.

statements.text: in non-vascular tissue
statements.explanation: Infection more readily becomes established in non-vascularised or necrotic tissue, since blood and its associated cells and oxygen form a primary host defence barrier.

statements.text: in patients with advanced malignancy
statements.explanation: Patients with advanced malignancy have an increased surgical-site infection rate, reflecting their compromised physiological status.

questions.stem: Important infection control measures shown to reduce the incidence of operation-related patient infections include

statements.text: restriction in the numbers and movement of theatre staff
statements.explanation: Restriction of theatre staff numbers and movement (likely related to airflow disturbance) has been shown to reduce operation-related infection rates.

statements.text: wearing of face masks
statements.explanation: Wearing of face masks has not been shown to significantly affect surgical site infection rates, so this statement is false.

statements.text: 12-hour rather than 24-hour preoperative skin shaving
statements.explanation: Hair clipping immediately before incision is associated with fewer wound infections than any form of razor shaving regardless of timing (12 vs 24 hours), so the specific 12-vs-24-hour shaving comparison is not the relevant factor and this statement is false as framed.

statements.text: cleansing of the skin in the operation field by antiseptics
statements.explanation: Cleansing the operative skin field with antiseptics reduces the microbial load and lowers subsequent wound infection rates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is MOST often found to be a contributing factor in patients with postoperative abdominal wound disruption?
questions.explanation: Local factors are more commonly a cause of postoperative wound disruption than general factors, although these latter can be important. Hypoproteinaemia and anaemia, if severe, may contribute, and advanced age is usually associated with other factors such as malnutrition or carcinoma. Local sepsis or a digestive fistula can contribute to wound necrosis. Adequate techniques of wound closure using strong nonabsorbable sutures can minimise the risk of disruption. Increased intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, sneezing, ileus, distension) is the most common contributor of those listed (B correct). Although all of the responses can contribute to wound dehiscence, increased intra- abdominal pressure (from coughing and straining, or from abdominal distension due to ileus), is the most common contributing factor of those listed (B).

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are adequate for sterilisation?

statements.text: Steam at 121oC for 15 minutes (autoclaving)
statements.explanation: Steam at 121°C for 15 minutes (autoclaving) is an accepted and effective method of sterilisation, since moist heat penetrates materials far more effectively than dry heat.

statements.text: Filtration through an 0.45µm pore size membrane
statements.explanation: Filtration through a 0.45 micron membrane removes most bacteria but does not remove smaller organisms such as mycoplasmas and viruses, so it is not adequate for sterilisation, making this statement false.

statements.text: Ethylene oxide gas for 24 hours
statements.explanation: Ethylene oxide gas exposure (typically at 54-60°C, 60-75% humidity, for at least 12 hours plus aeration) is an effective sterilisation method for heat-sensitive items, though the 24-hour figure in the statement somewhat overstates the typical minimum exposure time used.

statements.text: Boiling for 10 minutes
statements.explanation: Boiling for 10 minutes kills many vegetative bacteria but is inadequate against more resistant forms such as sporing bacilli, so this is not an adequate sterilisation method, making this statement false.

questions.stem: The skin is an unsatisfactory environment for many microbes because of its

statements.text: resident microbial flora
statements.explanation: The skin's resident microbial flora occupies available ecological niches, making it harder for transient or pathogenic organisms to establish, contributing to the skin's unfavourable environment for many microbes.

statements.text: alkaline pH
statements.explanation: The skin's surface is normally acidic (around pH 5.5), not alkaline, due to fatty acids, lactate and keratinisation products forming the 'acid mantle', so this statement is false.

statements.text: dryness
statements.explanation: The skin (in most areas) is normally dry, which is unsuitable for the growth of many microbes, contributing to its hostility as a microbial environment.

statements.text: mucus secretions
statements.explanation: Skin secretions (sweat, sebaceous) do not contain mucus; the acid mantle is instead made up of fatty acids, lactate and salt, so this statement is false.

questions.stem: In relation to antibiotics

statements.text: quinolones are well absorbed after oral administration
statements.explanation: Quinolones have good bioavailability and excellent body distribution after oral administration, with newer agents permitting once-daily dosing.

statements.text: aminoglycosides include vancomycin
statements.explanation: Vancomycin is a cell wall-active glycopeptide, structurally and mechanistically unrelated to the aminoglycosides, so this statement is false.

statements.text: some cephalosporins may induce bleeding problems following prolonged administration
statements.explanation: Prolonged cephalosporin use, particularly with agents bearing a methyl-thiotetrazole side chain (e.g. cefamandole, cefotetan), can reduce vitamin K levels and cause hypoprothrombinaemia and bleeding, especially in elderly or malnourished patients.

statements.text: piperacillin/tazobactam is effective therapeutically against MRSA
statements.explanation: MRSA are resistant to all beta-lactams, including piperacillin/tazobactam, because resistance is due to an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) rather than beta-lactamase production, so piperacillin/tazobactam is not effective against MRSA, making this statement false.

questions.stem: Therapeutically useful microbe/antimicrobial agent combinations include

statements.text: Bacteroides fragilis/metronidazole
statements.explanation: Bacteroides fragilis has remained universally susceptible to metronidazole (and also imipenem/meropenem and chloramphenicol), making this a genuinely useful combination.

statements.text: Staphylococcus aureus/piperacillin
statements.explanation: Over 80% of Staphylococcus aureus strains elaborate penicillinases, which destroy the activity of piperacillin (a penicillinase-labile penicillin) unless combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, so piperacillin alone is not a reliable therapeutic choice.

statements.text: Enterococcus faecalis/gentamicin
statements.explanation: Enterococci show inherent decreased susceptibility or resistance to aminoglycosides alone, though gentamicin plus a penicillin like ampicillin shows useful synergy; gentamicin by itself is not considered a reliable single-agent choice against Enterococcus faecalis.

statements.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae/imipenem
statements.explanation: Mycoplasmas lack a cell wall and are unaffected by cell-wall-active antimicrobials such as imipenem (a beta-lactam); the usual therapeutic choice for mycoplasma infections is a macrolide such as erythromycin.

questions.stem: Cephalosporins

statements.text: are active therapeutically against enterococci
statements.explanation: All cephalosporins show no therapeutic activity against enterococci; their widespread prophylactic and therapeutic use is thought to be one of the main reasons enterococci have emerged as significant hospital pathogens.

statements.text: are associated with greater allergic problems than penicillins
statements.explanation: Compared to penicillins, cephalosporins have always been significantly more resistant to beta-lactamase inactivation and are clearly less likely to induce allergic or hypersensitive reactions, with cross-reactivity in penicillin-allergic patients around 10% or less.

statements.text: have no action against Staphylococcus aureus
statements.explanation: First and second generation cephalosporins (e.g. cefuroxime) have excellent activity against Staphylococcus aureus, so this statement that they have no action against it is false.

statements.text: are generally more resistant to beta-lactamases than the penicillins
statements.explanation: Cephalosporins have always been significantly more resistant to beta-lactamase inactivation than the penicillins, which is the basis of their good activity against beta-lactamase-producing organisms like S. aureus.

statements.explanation: This cell-wall-active beta-lactam combination is ineffective against mycoplasmas, which do not possess a cell wall.

questions.stem: Regarding the treatment of infections by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

statements.text: vancomycin is the only reliable empiric therapy
statements.explanation: Vancomycin is the only antibiotic to which 100% of MRSA strains are consistently susceptible, making it the reliable empiric choice (though strains with reduced susceptibility are slowly emerging).

statements.text: coamoxyclav is useful for some strains
statements.explanation: MRSA strains are resistant to all beta-lactams, including coamoxyclav, because of the new low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP2a, so coamoxyclav is not useful for MRSA.

statements.text: imipenem is useful for some strains
statements.explanation: Imipenem is also a beta-lactam and is therefore ineffective against MRSA strains for the same PBP2a-mediated resistance reason.

statements.text: an antibiotic such as fusidic acid maybe useful for some strains
statements.explanation: Most community MRSA strains (unlike many hospital strains) are not multiresistant and remain susceptible to non-beta-lactam agents such as fusidic acid, cotrimoxazole, rifampicin, gentamicin and ciprofloxacin, usually used in combination.

questions.stem: In hospitals where MRSA are absent, acceptable antibiotics for hip replacement surgery prophylaxis include

statements.text: cephazolin alone
statements.explanation: First or second generation cephalosporins such as cephazolin have an ideal antibacterial spectrum against staphylococci for hip replacement prophylaxis, with a longer half-life and good bone penetration favoured by many institutions.

questions.stem: Antifungals therapeutically useful for Candida fungaemia in the post surgery patient include

statements.text: amphotericin B
statements.explanation: Amphotericin B (a polyene) is suitable for treating Candida fungaemia in surgical patients, particularly reserved for situations where white cell number or function is impaired, such as neutropenia.

statements.text: griseofulvin
statements.explanation: Griseofulvin's target is fungal nucleic acid synthesis and it is only active against dermatophytes (ringworm fungi), making it unsuitable for treating Candida fungaemia.

statements.explanation: Fluconazole (an azole) is suitable, and usually preferred over intravenous amphotericin B, for treating Candida infections in surgical patients because it is easier to administer and far less toxic.

statements.text: nystatin
statements.explanation: Nystatin (a polyene) is presently only available as a topical cream, ointment, or lozenge, and is not absorbed from the gut following oral administration, so it is not useful for treating systemic Candida fungaemia.

questions.stem: Adequate antibiotic prophylaxis for surgery involving the large bowel includes

statements.explanation: Amoxycillin plus metronidazole adequately covers Bacteroides fragilis via metronidazole, but is devoid of cover against E. coli (since at least half of strains are amoxycillin-resistant) or Staphylococcus aureus (since over 80% elaborate penicillinases that inactivate amoxycillin), so this combination is inadequate.

statements.text: tobramycin alone (parenterally)
statements.explanation: Tobramycin alone is devoid of any obligate anaerobe activity, despite being excellent against E. coli and S. aureus, making it inadequate alone; aminoglycosides are also best avoided due to potential potentiation of neuromuscular blockade by anaesthetic agents.

questions.stem: You are admitting a 70 year old man for an anterior resection of th rectum for carcinoma. He is otherwise in good health. What is the MOST appropriate DVT prophylaxis?
options: B. Heparin (unfractionated UFH or low molecular weight MWH) pre-operatively and until fully mobile.
C. Anti-embolus stockings and heparin (UFH or LMWH) pre-operatively and until fully mobile plus pneumatic compression in theatre.
D. Aspirin 100mg bd commencing one week before operation

questions.explanation: This is a high-risk patient (cancer, age 70). Early ambulation, aspirin and Macrodex infusion may be appropriate but each is inadequate as sole prophylaxis. questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with gallstones is admitted for an elective cholecystectomy. After the birth of her daughter three years ago she suffered a deep venous thrombosis in her left calf. At operation you plan to use pneumatic calf compression devices. What additional course of action would be most appropriate?
options: A. Start on warfarin immediately after the operation
B. Give intravenous heparin 1000 units/hr with the premedication and continue until mobile
C. Use anti-embolism stockings and apply from the time of premedication
D. No specific measures need to be taken other than early mobilisation
E. Give a 10 day course of subcutaneous heparin, starting at premedication
questions.explanation: Any action taken to reduce the risk of post-operative venous thrombo-embolic problems will be related to the presence of any risk factors. The patient described in this scenario has a total number of three risk factors, namely a past history of deep venous thrombosis (weighting 2) and she is about to undergo a laparoscopic procedure (weighting 1). She is classified as low risk and use of anti- embolism stockings or a low molecular weight heparin given subcutaneously is sufficient prophylaxis (C is correct, D is incorrect). The subcutaneous heparin would only need to be continued until the patient was mobile (E is incorrect). Intravenous heparin would be more suitable for a high risk patient, particularly one who had been on warfarin before the operation. The dose mentioned is in any event therapeutic rather than prophylactic (B is incorrect). There would be few circumstances where warfarin would be commenced immediately after an operation. If a patient had been on warfarin immediately prior to surgery, it would almost certainly have been stopped and the anticoagulation maintained in the interim with heparin. It is easier to reverse the effects of heparin than warfarin (A is incorrect).

statements.text: acne
statements.explanation: Acne is a recognised feature of long-term glucocorticoid use.

statements.text: hirsutism
statements.explanation: Hirsutism is a recognised feature of long-term glucocorticoid use, alongside other 'Cushinoid' features such as moon facies and centripetal fat redistribution ('buffalo hump').

statements.text: polycythaemia
statements.explanation: Glucocorticoids stimulate bone marrow stem cells including the erythroid series, which can produce polycythaemia, consistent with high-dose steroid use.

statements.explanation: Prednisone is metabolised to prednisolone, which has substantial mineralocorticoid agonist activity on the renal tubules, predisposing to hypernatraemia (typically accompanied by relative hypokalaemia rather than hyperkalaemia).

statements.explanation: Glucocorticoids cause hyperglycaemia and glucose intolerance due to insulin resistance, not hypoglycaemia, so this statement is false.

statements.explanation: Unlike oestrogenic and androgenic steroids, glucocorticoids per se do not cause hepatic dysfunction or hyperbilirubinaemia, so this statement is false.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Mr CC has cryptogenic cirrhosis and is admitted with peritonitis, for which an exploratory laparotomy is necessary. Which of the following drugs would have significantly altered clearance in this patient because of his cirrhosis?

statements.text: Frusemide
statements.explanation: Frusemide is excreted mainly by the kidney, not significantly affected by hepatic cirrhosis, so its clearance would not be significantly altered.

statements.text: Paracetamol
statements.explanation: Paracetamol is normally cleared by hepatic conjugation; in severe cirrhosis with decreased liver cell mass, this pathway is impaired and paracetamol toxicity (via the cytochrome P450 pathway) is significantly increased even at usually safe doses.

statements.text: Aspirin
statements.explanation: Aspirin is metabolised by plasma esterases then hepatically metabolised and conjugated with saturable kinetics; its half-life is increased in cirrhosis, particularly with significant intrahepatic shunting.

statements.text: Gentamicin
statements.explanation: Gentamicin is excreted by the kidney, not significantly affected by hepatic cirrhosis, so its clearance would not be significantly altered.

questions.stem: Mr CC has cryptogenic cirrhosis and is admitted with peritonitis, for which an exploratory laparotomy is necessary. The use of the following drugs during anaesthesia may lead to prolonged neuromuscular blockade in this man

statements.text: Suxamethonium
statements.explanation: Suxamethonium is metabolised by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase, the synthesis of which is decreased in liver disease, so its action may be prolonged in this patient.

statements.text: Atracurium
statements.explanation: Atracurium undergoes spontaneous nonenzymatic (Hoffman) degradation in plasma rather than depending on hepatic or cholinesterase metabolism, so its action is not prolonged by liver disease.

statements.text: Gallamine
statements.explanation: Gallamine is excreted almost entirely by the kidney, not affected by liver disease, so its action would not be prolonged in this patient.

statements.text: Mivacurium
statements.explanation: Mivacurium, like suxamethonium, is metabolised by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase, the synthesis of which is decreased in liver disease, so its action may be prolonged.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Mr CC has cryptogenic cirrhosis and is admitted with peritonitis, for which an exploratory laparotomy is necessary. If this patient developed cardiac failure and dysrhythmias post-operatively what would be the effect on the following drugs?

statements.text: the half-life of digoxin would be increased
statements.explanation: Digoxin's clearance is predominantly renal; its half-life is significantly increased by decreased renal perfusion, such as occurs with cardiac failure.

statements.text: the clearance of lignocaine would be increased
statements.explanation: Lignocaine has a high hepatic extraction ratio and flow-dependent clearance, so decreased hepatic perfusion in cardiac failure would decrease, not increase, its clearance.

statements.text: the half-life of vancomycin would be decreased
statements.explanation: Vancomycin's excretion depends entirely on glomerular filtration; decreased renal perfusion in cardiac failure would increase, not decrease, its half-life, increasing toxicity risk.

statements.text: the clearance of metronidazole would be decreased
statements.explanation: Metronidazole's hepatic clearance is not flow-dependent, so cardiac failure (which reduces hepatic blood flow) will not significantly alter its half-life or decrease its clearance.

questions.stem: In the following sequential developments in the 'metastatic, cascade' the second event to occur is
options: A. degradation of collagen and other matrix components
E. tumour cell interaction with platelets
questions.explanation: The ‘metastatic cascade’ concept is a useful one, in that it takes the whole process and itemises the steps in sequence from cancer cell ‘initiation’ through the concepts of genetic instability, selection of ‘metastatic subclones’, the necessity for acquisition of new characteristics of cells to break down extracellular matrix and so on. Detailed consideration of each of these areas is considered in preceding or following sections of the same chapter.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: In the following steps in the ‘metastatic cascade’, the second occurrence is
questions.explanation: The concept is, that before cancer cells can invade (or metastasise), there has to be: (1) initiation, (2) promotion, (3) proliferation (clonal expansion, growth) and diversification through subclone selection; via the inherent genetic instability of cancer cells, (4) selection of a ‘metastatic subclone’ (requires eg laminin and fibronectin receptor elaboration, ECM protease synthesis etc, locomotion capability and perhaps chemotaxis), before any of the possible responses (D), (E) or (B) come onto the scene (these last three are in that order of events).

questions.stem: Using a standard accepted model of theoretical growth of a cancer clone (30 doublings = 1 x 109 cells = 1 gram), this potential is never achieved because cells are lost to the proliferative pool when they

statements.text: enter the Go phase
statements.explanation: Cells entering the G0 (resting) phase exit the proliferative pool, which is one reason the theoretical maximum growth rate is never achieved clinically.

statements.text: are in the G1 phase
statements.explanation: Cells in the G1 phase are still considered part of the proliferative pool by definition, so this is not a reason for failing to achieve the theoretical maximum.

statements.text: enter the G2 phase
statements.explanation: Cells in the G2 phase are still considered part of the proliferative pool by definition, so this is not a reason for failing to achieve the theoretical maximum.

statements.text: differentiate

questions.stem: Experimental studies have shown that human cancer cells, when compared with normal tissues derived from labile cell populations

statements.text: have a higher percentage of terminally maturing cells
statements.explanation: In normal labile-cell epithelia, mitosing cells are present only in the basal layers and the bulk of cells are terminally maturing; this pattern is altered in cancer, so cancer cells do not show a higher percentage of terminally maturing cells compared to normal tissue.

statements.text: do not have a shorter cell cycle time
statements.explanation: Human cancer cells do not have a shorter cell cycle time compared with normal labile cell populations; their continued growth instead reflects an imbalance between cell production and cell loss.

statements.text: have a greater proportion of their cells in the replication cycle (growth fraction)
statements.explanation: Cancer cells do not necessarily have a greater proportion of cells in the replication cycle (growth fraction) compared with normal labile cell populations.

statements.text: replicate at a rate in excess of most labile cell populations
statements.explanation: Cancer cells do not replicate at a rate in excess of most labile cell populations; normal labile cells such as granulocytes and gut epithelia have very short life spans and high turnover.

questions.stem: There is a positive experimental and/or clinical correlation between metastatic potential of cancer cells and their

statements.text: elaboration of plasminogen activator
statements.explanation: Elaboration of plasminogen activator by tumour cells correlates with metastatic potential, contributing to breakdown of the intercellular matrix and creating space for invasion.

statements.text: blockade of fibronectin receptors on tumour cells
statements.explanation: Blockade of fibronectin receptors on tumour cells (which bind interstitial type I collagen/fibronectin) decreases, rather than correlates positively with, metastatic potential, so this statement is false.

statements.text: secretion of type IV collagenase
statements.explanation: Secretion of type IV collagenase, which degrades basement membrane collagen, correlates with metastatic potential.

statements.text: density of laminin receptors
statements.explanation: A higher density of laminin receptors, which bind tumour cells to basement membrane type IV collagen/laminin, correlates with metastatic potential.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Each of the following is true of carcinogenic initiation, except
options: E. can be active when given in divided doses
questions.explanation: This deals with oncogenic initiation and promotion. It relates to chemical carcinogenesis but is applicable, with modification, to radiation and viral oncogenesis. Rigid classification as 'complete' carcinogens (oncogens, but not oncogenes), initiators and promoters is conceptually useful, but not always easy. The concept is that initiators damage DNA in a fashion which is not susceptible to repair (either widely, or in individuals with genetic defect in DNA repair capability). Promoters then apparently ‘push’ the cell the extra step(s) to uncontrolled growth. This is central to understanding oncogenesis.

statements.explanation: Cellular enzyme systems can repair DNA damage, for example rapidly repairing single-strand breaks and, less promptly, some double-strand breaks; only irreparable damage may lead to cell death or the initial steps of oncogenesis, explaining why chemical DNA damage is not necessarily carcinogenic.

statements.explanation: Carcinogenesis induced by DNA viruses is a multistep process, even with highly oncogenic viruses, not a single-step ('single hit') process.

statements.text: may act by neutralising growth-inhibiting molecules
statements.explanation: DNA virus oncogenesis may act by neutralising growth-inhibiting molecules (such as tumour suppressor proteins).

statements.text: may involve incorporation of viral oncogene into host DNA
statements.explanation: DNA virus oncogenesis may involve stable incorporation of a viral oncogene into the host cell genome (and subsequent generations).

statements.text: may cause stimulation of function of growth-promoting protein(s)
statements.explanation: DNA virus oncogenesis may cause stimulation of function of growth-promoting proteins, depending on the specific virus involved.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: The effects of carcinogenic promoters are thought to be potentially reversible
statements.explanation: Promoters are not electrophilic and do not damage DNA themselves; their effects on clonal proliferation use existing normal growth-promoting pathways and can be lost if divided doses are too widely spaced, making their action potentially reversible.

statements.text: tumours do not eventuate if the ‘promoter-effective’ dose is applied prior to the application of the appropriate initiator.
statements.explanation: If a promoter-effective dose is applied before the appropriate initiator (i.e. with no prior DNA-damaging initiation event), no tumour develops, since promoters alone cannot initiate the irreversible DNA change required for carcinogenesis.

statements.text: angiogenesis factors
statements.explanation: Extracellular matrix breakdown products give rise to angiogenesis factors, promoting new blood vessel formation to support tumour growth.

statements.text: chemotaxis factors
statements.explanation: Extracellular matrix breakdown products give rise to chemotaxis factors, attracting cells relevant to tumour growth and spread.

statements.text: growth factors
statements.explanation: Extracellular matrix breakdown products give rise to growth factors that can stimulate tumour cell proliferation.

statements.text: a physical passage for tumour cell migration
statements.explanation: Matrix degradation creates physical space, providing a passage for tumour cell migration and invasion.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Carcinomas develop through ‘dedifferentiation’ of normal, differentiated, cells
statements.explanation: Cancers arise from mutations in the DNA of proliferating (dividing) cells, not from 'dedifferentiation' of terminally differentiated, non-dividing cells, since mutations cannot induce growth in cells that are not dividing.

statements.text: carcinomas result from repression of normal gene activity in differentiated, mature cells which revert to ‘immature’ cells.
statements.explanation: Most or all clinical cancers result from multiple sequential mutations in a clone of proliferating stem cells, rather than from repression of gene activity causing mature differentiated cells to revert to an immature state.

questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Under abnormal circumstances cells produce substances (eg hormones) which differ from their customary products
statements.explanation: Under abnormal conditions such as neoplasia, a cell may produce an inappropriate product, such as an ectopic hormone, that differs from its normal tissue-specific output.

statements.text: the DN repression in a differentiated cell is reversible
statements.explanation: Gene repression established during normal differentiation is often reversible; under abnormal conditions this reversal allows a differentiated cell to re-express genes (such as those for hormone production) normally repressed in that tissue, which explains the first statement.

questions.explanation: Thyroid papillary cancer is a major risk following childhood head and neck radiation, often for trivial problems. statements.explanation: Metaplasia is an adaptive response to chronic cell injury, occurring as environmental change induces differentiating stem-cell progeny to express different genes, producing a different phenotype.

statements.text: epithelial metaplasia does not revert to normal morphology following cessation of the causal injury.
statements.explanation: With removal of the causal injury, metaplastic cells die off and stem cells regenerate normal tissue under the now-normal environment, so metaplasia does in fact usually revert to normal morphology once the injury ceases, making this reasoning false.

questions.stem: Dysplastic melanocytic naevi

statements.text: very seldom occur on other than sun-exposed skin
statements.explanation: Dysplastic naevi, unlike ordinary moles, are common on sun-protected skin as well as sun-exposed skin, so this statement is false.

statements.text: usually have pale edges with a uniform central 'salmon pink' papule
statements.explanation: Dysplastic naevi are larger and irregular in outline and colour, lacking the distinct uniform 'salmon pink' pattern described, so this statement is false.

statements.text: most develop into malignant melanoma within two decades if not ablated
statements.explanation: Most dysplastic naevi are stable lesions; while they carry significant premalignant potential, the majority do not progress to malignant melanoma within two decades, so this statement is false.

statements.explanation: Dysplastic naevi show melanocytic atypia (dysplasia) and a superficial dermal lymphocytic infiltrate on histology.

questions.stem: Merkel cell carcinoma of the skin

statements.text: is an indolent ‘adnexal’ tumour resembling basal cell carcinoma in behaviour
statements.explanation: Merkel cell carcinoma has a formidably aggressive biology, unlike the indolent behaviour of basal cell carcinoma, so this statement is false.

statements.text: histologically resembles ‘oat cell’ bronchial carcinoma
statements.explanation: Merkel cell carcinoma histologically resembles 'oat cell' bronchial carcinoma and other neuroendocrine cancers such as carcinoid tumours and islet cell tumours.

statements.text: most commonly arises in axillae, groins or midline anterior abdominal skin
statements.explanation: Merkel cell carcinoma most commonly presents in the head and neck (and extremities), not the axillae, groins, or midline anterior abdominal skin, so this statement is false.

statements.explanation: Merkel cell carcinoma shows both neuroendocrine and epithelial differentiation on cell marker studies, consistent with its resemblance to neuroendocrine cancers.

questions.stem: Malignant melanoma

statements.text: is usually uniformly either black or amelanotic
statements.explanation: Malignant melanoma is characterised by irregularity of colour within individual lesions, not uniform black or amelanotic colouration, so this statement is false.

statements.text: may arise in diverse mucosal sites
statements.explanation: Malignant melanoma may arise in diverse mucosal sites, not only in the skin.

statements.text: usually has irregular ‘notched’ borders
statements.explanation: Malignant melanoma usually has an irregular, 'notched' border, reflecting its irregular growth pattern.

statements.text: prognosis is predicted most accurately by the mitotic rate
statements.explanation: Prognosis in malignant melanoma is determined most accurately by the nature and extent of the vertical growth phase (Breslow thickness), not by mitotic rate alone, so this statement is false.

questions.stem: Kaposi's sarcoma

statements.text: arises in skin and usually remains confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue
statements.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma, especially as part of AIDS, is an aggressive skin neoplasm that fairly rapidly disseminates to the viscera, rather than remaining confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue, so this statement is false.

statements.text: is less biologically aggressive when it occurs in HIV-positive individuals
statements.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma is more biologically aggressive, not less, when it occurs in HIV-positive individuals, rapidly disseminating to viscera as part of the AIDS syndrome, so this statement is false.

statements.text: presents as reddish, spreading and merging papules and plaques in the skin
statements.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma presents as reddish, spreading and merging papules and plaques in the skin.

statements.text: is a suppressor T lymphoproliferative disorder
statements.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma is an endothelial sarcoma of undefined histogenesis, not a suppressor T-lymphoproliferative disorder, so this statement is false.

questions.stem: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency may present with all of the following except
questions.explanation: The vertebrobasilar system supplies the medulla, pons, cerebellum, and occipital cortex: regions of the central nervous system concerned with balance, coordination of eye movements, and vision. Additionally, cranial nerve nuclei driving the muscles of the mouth and pharynx may be affected, causing swallowing difficulty and dysarthria. Since the major motor pathways to the limbs must pass through this territory, transient ischaemia may result in drop attacks without loss of consciousness, due to weakness of the lower limbs. Motor dysphasia (not always easy to distinguish from dysarthria) is due to lesions affecting Broca's motor speech area. The motor speech area is in the territory of the middle cerebral artery, and therefore is affected by carotid, but not vertebrobasilar, lesions. The exception i thus option E.

statements.explanation: Due to the erect posture, hydrostatic pressure increases progressively from the heart down to the distal arteries (some 30 mmHg higher at the inguinal ligament), and pulse-wave vibrational stress also increases distally, both contributing to greater wall stress and endothelial injury at more distal sites, explaining the distribution pattern.

questions.stem: According to current understanding, the third of the following stages to occur in the development of atherosclerosis is

B. platelet and monocyte synthesis and release of cytokine ‘growth factors’
C. smooth muscle cell migration into the intima
D. atrophy and degeneration of medial muscle and elastica
E. matrix vesicles initiate dystrophic calcification

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Right ventricular failure is most likely to be a long-term sequel of which cardiac pathology?
options: E. Stenosis of the left main coronary artery
questions.explanation: The right ventricle may fail secondary to pressure overload transmitted back from a failing left ventricle. This mechanism is prominent in mitral stenosis, where the left atrial pressure may be elevated twenty or more mmHg, thus effectively doubling right ventricular workload. Such great elevations in left atrial pressure are less common in aortic valve disease or ischaemia, and would only be seen in patients with severely decompensated failure and a grossly dilated left ventricle.

questions.stem: In a patient with rapidly progressing congestive cardiac failure, myocardial biopsy shows round cell infiltrates and tissue oedema. This would be consistent with
questions.explanation: Oedema with round cell infiltrates indicates an acute inflammatory process with an active immunological challenge in progress, as seen in viral myocarditis (D correct). The necrosis of infarction provokes a prominent neutrophil infiltration and the debris of dead myocytes is conspicuous. Thiamine deficiency is seen in starving alcoholics and extreme dieters: the lesion is biochemical, since thiamine forms a cofactor for enzymes in energy metabolism of glucose, and patients develop acute left ventricular failure which is promptly reversed by thiamine injection. Dilated cardiomyopathy, seen as an idiopathic state, or as a late sequel of viral myocarditis, or in chronically debilitated alcoholics, shows a biopsy picture of extensive fibrosis, rather than an active inflammatory process.

questions.stem: Stenoses in coronary atherosclerosis
options: A. in the left coronary are typically more diffuse than lesions than in the right
B. in the anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending) are usually distal
C. in the circumflex artery are usually distal
D. involve a worse prognosis for two-vessel disease than for untreated left main disease
E. usually spare the right posterior descending artery
questions.explanation: Patterns of coronary disease have very characteristic distributions. In the left coronary system, the stenoses are usually short and lesions of the (left) anterior interventricular and circumflex are usually proximal. Lesions on the right are more diffuse and distal, but usually spare the (right) posterior descending artery (E correct). Prognosis of untreated lesions worsens progressively with one, two or three arteries involved, but left main coronary artery disease is comparable to three-artery disease (worse than two).

questions.explanation: A large cardiac infarct three days old will show coagulative necrosis (A false). This typically excites a acute inflammatory reaction at its margins (B false), and may provoke the formation of a thrombus on the endocardial surface (C false). Cardiac infarcts typically show seepage of red cells among the muscle fibres (D false). Perivascular accumulation of lymphocytes is not a feature of the reaction to infarcts (E true).

questions.stem: With respect to myocardial ischaemia
options: A. acute unstable angina is usually precipitated by increased oxygen demand
B. angina pectoris is typically due to plaque disruption and platelet deposition

C. painless myocardial ischaemic episodes precipitated by emotional stress in patients with documented coronary occlusive lesions, are a recognised entity with similar prognostic implications t classical angina
D. angina in the absence of angiographically normal coronary vessels is moderately common
E. 'syndrome X' only occurs in patients with demonstrated single vessel lesions
questions.explanation: A and B are reversed - it is the acute coronary syndromes of myocardial infarction and unstable (crescendo) angina which are due to thrombosis, while classical angina is precipitated by increased myocardial workload in the presence of fixed reductions in calibre of major vessels. Not all ischaemia is painful - the mechanisms are poorly understood, but the prognostic implications are similar to symptomatic ischaemia: statement C is correct. Options D and E are inverted. Angina is rare in the absence of occlusive lesions: when it occurs it is known as 'syndrome X' and believed to be due to lesions in the microvasculature. 9 Dec 2002

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Sudden cardiac death is commonly
options: C. due to a ventricular tachyarrhythmia
D. prevented by class I antiarrhythmics
questions.explanation: Although any type of interference with the electrical or mechanical functions of the heart may lead to sudden death, in fact the overwhelmingly commonest cause is ventricular fibrillation - option C. Asystole may follow interruption to the conducting system below the AV node with occlusion of the left circumflex artery, but is less common than tachyarrhythmia. Cardiogenic shock is fortunately uncommon. When due to loss of a large zone of myocardium, its poor prognosis is not improved by early thrombolytic intervention. Antiarrhythmics are useful in treating arrhythmias, but disappointing when used prophylactically. Class Ic agents actually increase post-infarct mortality, emphasising the arrhythmogenic potential of antiarrhythmic drugs.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Consider the following statement and reason:

statements.text: Provocation by exercise and relief by rest are characteristic of limb pain due to arterial insufficiency
statements.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains the first statement. Resting skeletal muscle has very low requirements for blood flow: as little as 1% of the values seen i maximal exercise. Pain of arterial insufficiency is provoked by exercise, since the flow restriction of the stenosis results in diminished flow and pressure at the working muscles. This is the critical diagnostic feature of intermittent claudication thus statement and response are true and linked (A correct)

statements.text: exercise requires an increased blood flow to meet the metabolic needs of working muscle.

questions.explanation: . Other causes of lower limb pain, such as osteoarthritis, will not have the pattern of predictable onset with exercise and relief within a short period of rest. An arterial bruit at the site (and distal to) the stenosis, may not always be apparent at rest, but can appear during exercise as flow is increased due to the functional hyperaemia in working muscle, and flow velocity in the stenosis crosses the threshold for turbulence. Rest pain in arterial insufficiency is an extremely grave symptom, and in the light of the minimal nutritional requirements of resting muscle and connective tissues of the lower limb, indicates a profoundly reduced ability of the vasculature to supply blood flow.

questions.stem: Incompetence of the venous valve of the long saphenous trunk at the saphenofemoral junction, with competent leg and ankle perforators, is most likely to be associated with
options: E. none of the above features
questions.explanation: The presence of an incompetent saphenofemoral valve alone leads to varices in the long saphenous system. Since the ankle perforating vein valves are competent, the pressure in the superficial veins will fall on walking; and these patients tend not to develop the severe signs of venous hypertension (oedema, pigmentation, trophic changes, ulcers) seen in those suffering from incompetent valves in the ankle perforators. Typically, they suffer simple varicose veins (option D). The degree of pathology correlates better with the measured venous pressure during exercise and standing, than with the clinical assessment of venous valves.

statements.text: thrombosis is more frequent in th pelvic veins than in calf veins

questions.stem: Deep venous thrombosis is more common in patients with a history of any of the following except
options: C. surgery, especially abdominal, pelvic or hip, or immobilisation
D. obesity, old age, or past history
questions.explanation: Deep venous thrombosis can occur in any clinical setting, and pulmonary embolism is the commonest potentially preventable cause of death after major surgery. There is an impressive list of known risk factors, all connected more-or-less plausibly to either hypercoagulability or venous stasis. Among common conditions, anaemia is one of the few not conspicuously associated with DVT (E True). Polycythaemia, as a cause of elevated blood viscosity, is a known association with DVT.

options: A. pain, induration, heat and tenderness along the involved vein
questions.explanation: Thrombophlebitis of superficial veins is often caused by trauma, cannulation, or a nearby infection. Its clinical signs are obvious. The process tends to remain localised to a single vein system: therefore, venous hypertension of the limb with oedema does not usually occur (option B).

questions.topic_label: General Path + Tissue Response to Injury — Haemodynamic Disorders, Thrombosis
questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Lymphoedema occurs when lymphatic vessels fail to remove from the interstitial space
options: E. none of the above components
questions.explanation: The question does not ask what lymphatics remove, but rather, which of the things that they normally remove is the cause of oedema when lymphatic function is absent. Interstitial fluid pressure depends on the equilibrium of Starling forces: the hydrostatic pressure in the capillary pushing fluid out, and the osmotic pressure of plasma proteins pulling fluid back into the capillary. Capillaries are generally fully permeable to salt, water and small molecules, but nearly completely impermeable to proteins like albumin. The 'nearly' is the catch. Lymphatics remove a small amount of interstitial fluid, including the protein that leaks slowly through capillaries. In the absence of lymphatic function, that protein accumulates, abolishing the colloid osmotic pressure gradient from blood to interstitial fluid which normally pulls fluid back into the capillary. The result is oedema - lymphoedema. Thus, option C is th required answer. RESPIRATORY

questions.stem: Patients with significant pulmonary embolism usually show on investigation all except
options: A. ECG changes with ST depression and T inversion
B. defects in pulmonary perfusion scans
D. arterial hypoxaemia with increased A-a oxygen tension difference
E. normal chest X-ray, at least initially
questions.explanation: Investigations are also difficult in pulmonary embolism. Disparity between the ventilation and perfusion scans in nuclear medicine techniques is highly specific and usefully sensitive for haemodynamically significant emboli. The ventilation-perfusion mismatch is apparent on blood gas investigations, where there is an alveolar to arterial oxygen tension difference. Chest X-ray is initially unhelpful; the wedge-shaped radiological opacity occurring later as the lung in the territory of the obstructed artery consolidates. ECG changes are seen in a small minority of patients - those with severe right ventricular overload from pulmonary hypertension. Thus, option A is inconsistent with th majority picture, and is therefore the required answer.

questions.source: RACS legacy question bank (Eugene Lim compilation, c.2005-2006), original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.
questions.stem: Reduction in the mortality of acute pancreatitis is most likely to result from
options: C. early correction of fluid and electrolyte losses.
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis exhibits a spectrum of severity. Severe acute pancreatitis is accompanied by hypovolaemia with massive sequestration of fluid and electrolytes in the abdomen and retroperitoneum. Early correction of such losses is of major importance in treatment, and is the most likely of the responses to influence mortality (C correct). Aprotinin and glucagon have been widely used in treatment, but have not been demonstrated effective in influencing mortality in clinical trials (A and B incorrect). Parenteral nutrition is helpful in treating the complications of acute pancreatitis such as prolonged ileus and abscess formation, but is not so relevant to early mortality (D incorrect). Peritoneal lavage and dialysis have a role in management of acute pancreatitis (particularly when acute pancreatitis is diagnosed at operation) and in the management of local and systemic complications (pancreatic abscess and renal failure). There is no evidence that they reduce the early mortality (E incorrect).

questions.stem: Which of the following problems does NOT accompany the use of a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube inserted for balloon tamponade of bleeding oesophageal varices?
questions.explanation: The Sengstaken-Blakemore tube can give effective control of acute bleeding from oesophageal varices. There are a of hazards and complications of its use. Aspiration or asphyxia during insertion, oesophageal pressure necrosis or rupture, and rebleeding after balloon deflation are the most important. The tube should preferably be inserted, and the patient managed, in an intensive-care environment. Vagal-induced bradycardia is not a complication. Stimulation of afferent vagal fibres related to the oesophagus or stomach does not evoke cardio-inhibitory reflexes, whereas hypovolaemic tachycardia is common. E is thus the correct response.

questions.stem: Colonic epithelial neoplasia is considered as not having significant metastatic potential if adequate histological examination shows

statements.explanation: Carcinoma in situ within an adenoma is, for pragmatic purposes, still considered a benign lesion that has not yet acquired the capacity to metastasise.

statements.explanation: Because lymphatic channels are largely absent from colonic mucosa, intramucosal carcinoma (focal carcinoma confined within an adenoma with severe dysplasia) is regarded as having little or no metastatic potential.

statements.explanation: Invasion of adenocarcinoma into the submucosa indicates that the tumour has crossed into tissue with lymphatic channels and has acquired real metastatic potential, so this lesion does have significant metastatic potential, making the statement false.

statements.explanation: Invasive adenocarcinoma reaching the superficial muscularis propria, even without demonstrable vascular or lymphatic permeation, has by definition invaded beyond the submucosa and carries real metastatic potential, so this statement is false.

questions.stem: The best survival with thyroid neoplasia is seen with
questions.explanation: Papillary cancer of the thyroid has a very good medium and even long term outlook, even in the presence of disseminated disease. Familial medullary cancer also has an excellent prognosis; this is not shared by the sporadic (non-familial) form of medullary cancer, which also has marked differences in clinical presentation. questions.stem: Prostate cancer is best diagnosed by
options: B. prostate specific antigen (PSA) serum levels
C. transrectal ultrasound of the prostate and biopsy
D. a combination of the above three responses
E. cystoscopy and endoscopic biopsy of the prostate
questions.explanation: When patients are first seen in the consulting rooms wishing a prostate check up, a digital rectal examination and PSA are often done to work-up symptoms or possibly as a routine prostate check. The definitive form of diagnosis, however, is with a transrectal ultrasound of the prostate with several biopsies. Diagnosis is best made by a combination of the three previous responses A, B & C (D is correct Biopsies are taken from the base, mid, and apex of each lobe of the prostate gland and submitted for histopathologic review. Many prostate cancers are isoechoic and hence are unable to be clearly identified on ultrasound, but some are associated with a hypoechoic nodule and hence can be targeted specifically if identified on ultrasound. There is very little, if any place, for a cystoscopy and endoscopic biopsy in the diagnosis of the vast majority of prostate cancers. As mentioned earlier, most cancers begin in the peripheral zone rather than in the periurethral zone and hence are unlikely to be sampled endoscopically (E False).

questions.stem: Common occurrences in advanced prostate cancer include

statements.text: spinal cord compression
statements.explanation: The most common are problems in advanced hormone-refractory prostate cancer and are associated with ongoing progression of bony metastatic disease as well as morbidity related to local spread. Hence ongoing bone pain is an issue and if affecting the thoracic/lumbar cord may lead to cord compression and to a rapid onset of paraparesis and paraplegia in affected individuals (1 True)

statements.text: haematuria
statements.explanation: This needs prompt treatment with urgent radiotherapy, or if unsuccessful urgent decompression laminectomy. Other strategies to assist in the management of bone pain include local radiotherapy, chemotherapy using mitozantrone and steroids, administration of radioactive strontium or palladium, referral to palliative care team and administration of analgesia (for example, MS Contin). The other problems relate to local growth of tumour, which include ongoing lower urinary tract symptoms, such as hesitancy, diminishing urinary stream, frequency, and nocturia (which may require palliative TURP) as well as haematuria due to the fragility of the neoplastic blood vessels (which may require cystoscopy and diathermy) (2 True)

statements.text: jaundice from hepatic metastase
statements.explanation: Hepatic and lung metastases are uncommon in advanced prostate cancer, although they may occur; but require palliation far less frequently than the previously mentioned problems (3 & 5 False)

statements.text: renal failure from bilateral ureteric obstruction
statements.explanation: As the tumour infiltrates the base of the bladder, bilateral ureteric obstruction is a common accompaniment of the disease requiring endoscopic manipulation in the form of nephrostomies and ureteric stents (4 True)

statements.text: respiratory distress and pneumonia secondary to lung metastases . Figure 10 - Semi-horizontal cross-section through prostate and rectum
statements.explanation: Hepatic and lung metastases are uncommon in advanced prostate cancer, although they may occur; but require palliation far less frequently than the previously mentioned problems (3 & 5 False)

questions.stem: Concerning prostate specific antigen (PSA)

statements.text: PSA is a glycoprotein secreted by prostate cells into the ejaculate
statements.explanation: Prostate specific antigen is a glycoprotein secreted by the prostate cells into the ejaculate (1 True)

statements.text: PSA serum levels are almost always raised in prostate cancer
statements.explanation: whose functions is to assist in the breaking down of gel proteins within the ejaculate - leading to liquefaction. Small quantities of prostate specific antigen leak into the peripheral circulation and henc can be detected on serum studies. Prostate specific antigen is not always elevated in the presence prostate cancer (2 False)

statements.text: PSA serum levels are unaffected by age of the patient
statements.explanation: As one would expect, the degree of benign prostatic hyperplasia tends to increase with age - one would also expect prostatic specific antigen levels to similarly increase with age, and age specific levels have been designed by many laboratories to take this factor into account (3 False)

statements.text: PSA serum levels may be elevated in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis or prostatic infarct
statements.explanation: and up to 20% of cancers may be missed if relying on prostate specific antigen levels alone. Digital rectal examination must, therefore, be done in all patients who wish a check up of their prostate. Prostate specific antigen levels can be elevated with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis and prostatic infarct and hence 70-80% of men with mildly elevated levels will, in fact, have one of these conditions rather than prostate cancer (4 True)

statements.text: PSA is universally endorsed and recommended as a screening test for prostate cancer
statements.explanation: The use of prostate specific antigen as a formal screening test for prostate cancer is controversial. It is endorsed by the American Urologic Association as well as the American Cancer Society, but it is not endorsed in many other countries including Australia and New Zealand (5 False)

questions.stem: What factors may influence choice of initial treatment for prostate cancer?

statements.text: age of patient
statements.explanation: Various factors influence the choice of therapy for localised prostate cancer. An older man, in particular, over 70 years of age, especially within the presence of co-morbid illnesses is more likely to die of those co-morbid illnesses rather than from the prostate cancer. Therefore, the expected ten-year life expectancy of the patient must be taken into account if active therapy is being considered. Grade of the tumor plays a major role, as a well-differentiated cancer has excellent 10-15 year cause-specific survival regardless of therapy (1, 2 & 5 True)

statements.text: co-morbid illnesses
statements.explanation: Various factors influence the choice of therapy for localised prostate cancer. An older man, in particular, over 70 years of age, especially within the presence of co-morbid illnesses is more likely to die of those co-morbid illnesses rather than from the prostate cancer. Therefore, the expected ten-year life expectancy of the patient must be taken into account if active therapy is being considered. Grade of the tumor plays a major role, as a well-differentiated cancer has excellent 10-15 year cause-specific survival regardless of therapy (1, 2 & 5 True)

statements.text: patient preference
statements.explanation: Moderate and poorly differentiated tumors do show a survival advantage of treatment over no treatment and hence is imperative that one identifies a patient with these grades of tumors before contemplating active therapy. Patient preference also plays a major role in the choice of therapy for localised prostate cancer (3 True)

statements.text: doctor preference
statements.explanation: The treatment of prostate cancer is commonly associated with impotence, in the case of surgery a low but definite risk of incontinence, and in the case of radiotherapy a low but definite risk of rectal irritation, diarrhea and rectal bleeding. No early treatment, as a preferred first option, clearly preserves rectal function, continence and erectile ability and hence many patients may choose no initial therapy to avoid the side effects of treatment even if it may ultimately compromise long-term survival. Doctors' preference should play a relatively minor role in the choice of therapy for the patient in these circumstances (4 False)

statements.text: grade of the cancer
statements.explanation: Various factors influence the choice of therapy for localised prostate cancer. An older man, in particular, over 70 years of age, especially within the presence of co-morbid illnesses is more likely to die of those co-morbid illnesses rather than from the prostate cancer. Therefore, the expected ten-year life expectancy of the patient must be taken into account if active therapy is being considered. Grade of the tumor plays a major role, as a well-differentiated cancer has excellent 10-15 year cause-specific survival regardless of therapy (1, 2 & 5 True)

questions.stem: Hormone manipulation for prostate cancer can be optimally administered by

statements.text: orchidectomy f
statements.explanation: Prostate cancer is a known hormonally sensitive cancer in 80% of cases and will respond to testosterone deprivation therapy. The bulk of the male androgens come from the testes and hence either a surgical castration in the form of a bilateral orchidectomy or a medical castration in the form of an LHRH agonist, for example, Zoladex (10.8mg subcutaneously three-monthly) or Lucrin depot (22.5mg IM three-monthly) are acceptable alternatives (1 & 2 True)

statements.text: LHRH agonist
statements.explanation: Prostate cancer is a known hormonally sensitive cancer in 80% of cases and will respond to testosterone deprivation therapy. The bulk of the male androgens come from the testes and hence either a surgical castration in the form of a bilateral orchidectomy or a medical castration in the form of an LHRH agonist, for example, Zoladex (10.8mg subcutaneously three-monthly) or Lucrin depot (22.5mg IM three-monthly) are acceptable alternatives (1 & 2 True)

statements.text: antiandrogen therapy
statements.explanation: There is no need to add an t LHRH to an orchidectomy, as they serve the same function, and side-effects are identical (namely, hot flushes, impotence, weight gain, gynaecomastia and mood disturbances). Oral anti-androgen therapy alone has generally not been recognised as adequate treatment (3 False)

statements.text: orchidectomy plus antiandrogen therapy
LHRH plus antiandrogen therapy

questions.explanation: although the steroidal anti-androgen Cyproterone Acetate (100mg three times a day) may be used as monotherapy in selective cases. The non-steroidal anti-androgens, namely, Flutamide (250mg orally TDS), Nilutamide (150-300mg daily), and Bicalutamide (50mg a day) are not as effective as monotherapy in current dosage schedules. The anti-androgens have the theoretic advantage that they may eradicate the additional 5-10% of male androgens that are derived from the adrenal gland rather than from the testes. Hence there has been considerable debate, as to whether combined androgen blockade, in the form of an orchidectomy, or LHRH agonist in conjunction with an anti- androgen may provide superior results to an orchidectomy or LHRH agonist alone. Although some randomised controlled trials do show a slight survival advantage in the combined androgen blockade group, this data overall has not been conclusive with many conflicting reports showing no benefit (4 5 False). Figure 9 shows the hormonal influences affecting the prostate cell and the site of action of some drugs used in treatment of prostate cancer. LHRH analogues inhibit pituitary secretion and diminish testosterone secretion, as does orchidectomy. Anti-androgens act peripherally to block testosterone action on androgen receptors. Agents such as ketoconazole and aminoglutethamide inhibit circulating androgens.

questions.stem: The following statements are correct regarding treatment of testicular tumours

statements.text: seminoma is highly radiosensitive
statements.explanation: Seminoma is exquisitely radiosensitive (1 True)

statements.text: most centres adopt a management policy of intense surveillance without additional therapy after orchidectomy for organ-confined seminoma
most centres adopt a management policy of intense surveillance without additional therapy after orchidectomy for organ-confined non-seminomatous germ cell tumour
statements.explanation: and for stage I and early stage II tumors 95% of patients are cured with retroperitoneal low dose radiotherapy. (Delivery of 25-30 Gray to the retroperitoneal and ipsilateral pelvic lymph nodes). Response 2 is false. Seminomas of high stage and with bulky retroperitoneal nodes or distant metastatic disease are treated with systemic chemotherapy using a regime of Bleomycin, Etoposide and Cis-platinum. Four cycles of treatment, three weeks apart, are associated with cure rates of >90% in this group of patients. The treatment of node negative disease is more controversial. 'Watchful-waiting' in this group has several disadvantages: Natural History: 25% of patients can be expected to relapse, usually with retroperitoneal nodal disease - in seminoma relapse occurs up to 5 years after orchidectomy. Ease of surveillance: Tumour markers are generally not elevated so surveillance is with CT imaging alone - this is quite a lot of radiation with regular CT for 5 years. Patient compliance also becomes a factor. Low dose radiotherapy to the retroperitoneum is well tolerated and minimises the risk of recurrence to <5%. Conclusion - Radiotherapy to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes for stage I disease is the preferred treatment in the vast majority of centres. Stage 1 non-seminomatous germ cell tumour is treated with surveillance after orchidectomy (3 True)

statements.text: residual masses in the chest and retroperitoneum after chemotherapy for non-seminoma are best managed by surgical resection
a solid mass arising within the testis has a 50% risk of being malignant
statements.explanation: Seventy-five per cent of patients with stage 1 NSGCT are cured with inguinal orchidectomy alone. Twenty-five per cent of patients relapse, usually in the retroperitoneal lymph nodes within two years. For this reason close follow-up with chest x-rays, CT, and tumour markers on clinical examination are appropriate. Tumour markers are checked six-weekly on clinical examination and chest x-rays and CT scans are checked three-monthly in the first year; with gradually diminishing intensity of follow-up over the subsequent two to three years. The majority of relapses occur within the first year and many cases of residual disease are detected by failure of tumor markers to normalise following inguinal orchidectomy. Overall in this group 25% of patients will develop recurrent disease. This risk increases to 45-50% in patients with embryonal cancer, with vascular invasion present in the inguinal orchidectomy specimen, or with a higher T stage. In patients who develop recurrent disease the appropriate treatment in the first instance is chemotherapy, again, initially with four cycles of BEP. Greater than 90% of patients can expect to be cured. (Response 4 is true) High stage NSGST is treated initially following orchidectomy with chemotherapy. If residual retroperitoneal mass exists despite chemotherapy and tumour marker normalisation, retroperitoneal lymph nodes dissection is required. Twenty per cent of these masses contain residual tumour, 40% mature teratoma, and 40% fibrosis. (Mature teratoma is generally benign but may cause local compression to neighbouring structures and can rarely undergo malignant degeneration.) Overall, 70% of patients with high volume disease are cured with chemotherapy +/- retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. Residual chest masses similarly are best excised. The risk of malignancy is very high in patients with a solid testicular mass (5 False)

questions.stem: A 45 year old patient has an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for proven gall stones. No problems occurred and the visualisation was good. Operative cholangiography was performed and considered normal. Twelve hours after operation the temperature is 39oC and pulse rate is 110 per minute. You would suspect as the MOST likely cause
options: D. reaction to the contrast medium.
questions.explanation: After an upper abdominal operation such as elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy without bile duct exploration, the commonest complication is postoperative atelectasis, which is especially common in smokers or those with pre-existing chest disease. Atelectasis commonly presents within the first 12-24 hours after surgery with fever and tachycardia, often without obvious clinical findings in the chest (A correct). It is thus the most likely of thediagnoses listed. You would of course need to consider operative complications as well! Intraperitoneal bile leak is more likely to occur when the bile duct has been explored, but can follow simple cholecystectomy as a result of leakage from the liver bed or due to the cystic duct clip(s) slipping. Clinical presentation is often delayed until 24 hours or more after operation, and presentation may be with abdominal signs of varying degree associated with shock. Cholangitis is rare after elective cholecystectomy without bile duct exploration. The frequency of infected bile rises in operations for acute cholecystitis and with bile duct stones. Reaction to the contrast medium is les common than atelectasis; and wound infection does not usually present within the first 12 hours.

questions.stem: From an epidemiological viewpoint, what factors are known to be associated with the development of prostate cancer?

statements.text: country of origin
statements.explanation: There is a significant variation in the incidence of prostate cancer depending on the country of origin of the patient, with Asian countries typically having an extremely low incidence of prostate cancer an most developed western countries having a high incidence (1 True)

statements.text: smoking
statements.explanation: The incidence, however, of microscopically detected cancers at autopsy are similar throughout all countries; and hence prostate cancer in a western country tends to progress to a clinical stage as opposed to Asian countries. Migration affects this incidence, as a patient moves from a country of low incidence to high incidence they adopt the incidence of their host country. Obviously, diet has been implicated - but not proven - as a possible explanation for this differing incidence depending on country of origin (3 False?). Food substances that have been implicated include dietary fat, isoflavin ingestion (commonly found in soy products), and lycopenes (commonly found in tomato base products). Other possible explanation include exposure to ultraviolet light as those countries with minimal exposure to ultraviolet light such as the Scandinavian countries or those races that absorb vitamin D poorly (eg African-Americans) have a significant higher incidence of prostate cancer compared to their counterparts. There is no evidence that smoking is related to prostate cancer (2 False)

statements.text: diet
family history
statements.explanation: Family history has been conclusively shown to be associated with the incidence of prostate cancer with a two-fold incidence of prostate cancer with one first degree relative affected and up to eight to nine times increased risk if two first degree male relatives are affected (4 True)

statements.text: presence of lower urinary tract symptoms
statements.explanation: The presence of symptoms is not associated with the development of prostate cancer (5 False)

questions.explanation: as most studies have identified equal number of men with and without symptoms who have been diagnosed with the disease, despite the fact that symptoms was the most common reason why men sought to have their prostates checked.

questions.stem: At present, the most useful method of epidemiological investigation of staphylococcal infections is to determine
questions.explanation: The classical method of 'typing' staphylococci (both Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase negative species) in epidemiological investigations is phage typing (D true) although other molecular techniques are slowly being developed (eg plasmid analysis, chromosomal DNA analysis) as are antibiogram analyses for coagulase negative strains. Colony and colour variation is of little use as most colonies look the same (A false), while the presence or absence of the enzyme coagulase simply serves to delineate the heterogenous species S. aureus from the remaining 20 or so species (C false). Serological procedures have not been adopted for investigating outbreaks of staphylococcal sepsis (E false) except perhaps for determining the presence of a high level of antibody against cell wall teichoic acids as an indication of chronic staphylococcal infection (eg osteomyelitis). M proteins are antiphagocytic virulence factors in streptococci; they have been used in streptococcal typing schemes but are not present on staphylococci (B false).

options: A. the absence of an hypothesis
C. an hypothesis that no relationship exists

E. an hypothesis that a negative relationship exists A null hypothesis is a fundamental statistical tool comparing two events; and represents the hypothesis that no relationship exists between the two events. The hypothesis is then tested and either confirmed or refuted.

questions.stem: What is the least mobile part of the uterus?
questions.explanation: The cervix is the least mobile part of the uterus because of the passive support provided by the attached condensations of the endopelvic fascia (ligaments), which may also contain smooth muscle. The ligaments are the cardinal (transverse cervical) and the utero sacral. Cardinal ligament: extends form the supravaginal cervix and lateral parts of the fornix of the vagina to the lateral wall of the pelvis. Uterosacral ligaments: pass superiorly and slightly posteriorly from the sides of the cervix to the middle of the sacrum

questions.stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding inguinal hernias?
options: A. Direct inguinal hernias are more common than indirect inguinal hernias
B. Indirect inguinal hernias traverse the inguinal canal within the process vaginalis
C. Indirect inguinal hernias commonly pass into the scotum
D. Direct inguinal hernias occur as a result of a weakness of the anterior abdominal wall
questions.explanation: Characteristics of Inguinal hernias: Direct: Acquired weakness of the anterior abdominal wall, less common than direct, exits from abdominal cavity through peritoneum plus transversalis fascia, passes through the or around inguinal canal, via superficial ring, lateral cord, rarely enters scrotum. Direct hernias herniate medially to the inferior epigastric artery Direct inguinal hernias RIP through Hasselbach's triangle (R - rectus abdominis, I - inferior epigastric artery, P - Puopart's ligament = inguinal ligament). Indirect: Congenital weakness-patency of the process vaginalis, more common than direct hernias (2/3 or 3/4 of all inguinal hernias), exits from the abdominal cavity through peritoneum of persistent process vaginalis plus all 3 fascial coverings of cord/round ligaments, traverses inguinal canal within process vaginalis via superficial ring inside cord, commonly passing into scrotum/labium majora. Remember indirect hernias herniate laterally to the inferior epigastric artery

questions.stem: Regarding the anatomy of the spleen, which is CORRECT?
options: A. The approximate size of the spleen is 12cm long and 7 cm wide
B. The spleen is often palpable through the anterolateral abdominal wall
C. The diaphragmatic surface of the spleen is concave to fit the convexity of the diaphragm.
D. Lymph drainage of the spleen is via the pancreaticoduodenal nodes
questions.explanation: The spleen is ovoid, purplish, pulpy mass. The spleen is usually the size of ones fist but can vary considerably. The approximate size is 12cm long and 7 cm wide. The diaphragmatic surface of the spleen is convexly curved to fit the concavity of the diaphragm. The anterior and superior borders of the spleen are sharp and often notched whereas the inferior and posterior borders are rounded. The spleen is seldom palpable through the anterolateral abdominal wall unless it is enlarged. The relations of the spleen: anterior=stomach, posterior=left part of the diaphragm, inferiorly=left colic flexure and medially=left kidney. The arterial supply of the spleen is from the splenic artery, the largest branch of the celiac trunk. Venous drainage is via the splenic vein, which joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. Lymph drainage=pancreaticosplenic nodes. Nerve supply is derived from the celiac plexus and is vasomotor in function.
questions.source: iMeducate question bank, original phrasing preserved per fair-use educational transcription.

questions.stem: Referred pain from pancreatitis is felt at what level?
questions.explanation: The pain fibres accompany the sympathetic supply so that the pancreatic pain may radiate in the distrubution of the thoracic dermatomes T6-T10

questions.stem: Regarding the relations of the ureter, which of the following is false?
options: A. It crosses the sacro iliac joint at the bifurication of the iliac vessels
B. It crosses the vas deferens in males
C. The gonadal vessels cross over the ureters
D. It runs down the tips of the transverse processes of lumbar spine
questions.explanation: The ductus deferens crosses above the ureter and then runs medially to it. "Bridge over water" Note: In the old (now non- prescribed TB: the ureters lie medial to the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae) The new prescribed textbook: the ureters occupy a sagittal plane that intersects the tips of the transverse process of the lumbar vertebrae The wording although different reflects the same thing: the ureters overlie the tips of the transverse processes

questions.stem: Which of the following structures pass through the lesser sciatic foramen?
